disease.name: Fatty Liver Disease
disease.scientific_name: Hepatic Steatosis / Metabolic dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) / Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) / Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD)
disease.icd_10_code: K76.0 (Fatty (change of) liver, not elsewhere classified — NAFLD); K70.0 (Alcoholic fatty liver); K70.1 (Alcoholic hepatitis); K70.3 (Alcoholic cirrhosis of liver); K76.89 (Other specified diseases of liver); Z71.89 (Fatty liver NEC)

overview.description: Fatty liver disease is a broad spectrum of liver conditions characterised by abnormal accumulation of triglycerides (fat) within hepatocytes (liver cells), defined as hepatic fat content exceeding 5% of liver weight or fat present in more than 5% of hepatocytes on biopsy. It encompasses two major entities: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) — recently renamed Metabolic dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) in 2023 — occurring in the absence of significant alcohol consumption and driven by metabolic syndrome; and Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD) — caused by chronic excessive alcohol consumption. NAFLD/MASLD is the most common chronic liver disease globally, affecting approximately 25-30% of adults worldwide and representing a silent epidemic closely linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. The spectrum ranges from simple steatosis (benign fat accumulation) to steatohepatitis (fat + inflammation + injury), fibrosis, cirrhosis, and in some cases hepatocellular carcinoma.
overview.affected_organ: Liver (primary); also affects cardiovascular system, kidneys, and metabolic function systemically
overview.global_prevalence: NAFLD/MASLD: ~25-30% of adults globally; ~38% in Middle East and South America; ~27% in Asia; ~24% in Western Europe. India: estimated 9-32% (rising rapidly). ALD: major public health burden globally — alcohol is the third leading cause of preventable disease globally.
overview.age_group: NAFLD affects all ages including children; peak prevalence in adults 40-64 years; paediatric NAFLD rising alarmingly (3-10% in children, up to 35-40% in obese children). ALD peaks in 30-60 year age group.
overview.sex_ratio: NAFLD: similar prevalence in men and women overall; men more likely to develop NASH and advanced fibrosis; post-menopausal women see increased risk. ALD: men more commonly affected; women develop more severe disease at lower alcohol consumption levels (female vulnerability — smaller body mass, lower alcohol dehydrogenase activity).
overview.is_curable_note: Early-stage NAFLD (simple steatosis) is fully reversible with lifestyle changes. Advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis have limited reversibility but progression can be halted.
overview.emerging_crisis: WHO projects MASLD will become the leading cause of liver transplantation globally by 2030, overtaking viral hepatitis

nomenclature_update_2023.consensus: Delphi Consensus 2023 — agreed by major hepatology societies globally (EASL, AASLD, ALEH, AISF)
nomenclature_update_2023.rationale: MASLD better reflects the metabolic pathogenesis; removes stigmatising 'non-alcoholic' label; encompasses cardiometabolic risk factors in the definition

subtypes.MASL: Metabolic-Associated Steatotic Liver (simple steatosis without significant inflammation) — previously NAFL
subtypes.MASH: Metabolic-Associated Steatohepatitis (steatosis + lobular inflammation + hepatocyte ballooning) — previously NASH
subtypes.MetALD: Metabolic-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease with greater than moderate alcohol consumption — new category bridging MASLD and ALD
subtypes.ALD: Alcoholic Liver Disease — retained for predominantly alcohol-driven liver disease

nomenclature_update_2023.masld_criteria: Hepatic steatosis + at least ONE cardiometabolic risk factor: BMI ≥25 (≥23 in Asians), OR type 2 diabetes, OR blood pressure ≥130/85, OR triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, OR HDL <40 (men) or <50 (women) mg/dL
nomenclature_update_2023.clinical_note: Both NAFLD and MASLD terms used in this dataset — MASLD is the preferred current term; older literature uses NAFLD

types.name: Simple Hepatic Steatosis (MASL / NAFL)
types.description: The earliest and most common form — fat accumulation in hepatocytes (triglycerides) exceeding 5% without significant inflammation or hepatocyte injury. Characteristically asymptomatic. Liver function tests may be normal or mildly elevated. Most patients have simple steatosis and will NOT progress to advanced disease. However, ~20-25% may progress to steatohepatitis if metabolic risk factors persist uncontrolled.
types.histology: Macrovesicular steatosis in ≥5% of hepatocytes; no significant lobular inflammation; no hepatocyte ballooning; no Mallory-Denk bodies
types.prognosis: Generally benign; reversible with weight loss and metabolic control; low risk of progression with lifestyle intervention
types.management: Lifestyle modification (weight loss 5-7%, Mediterranean diet, exercise); treatment of metabolic comorbidities

types.name: Metabolic-Associated Steatohepatitis (MASH / NASH)
types.description: The progressive, inflammatory form of fatty liver disease — the 'dangerous' phenotype with potential for irreversible fibrosis and cirrhosis. Characterised by the histological triad of: (1) steatosis, (2) lobular inflammation (neutrophilic and mononuclear infiltration), and (3) hepatocyte ballooning (cytoplasmic swelling and injury — the pathognomonic feature). May progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
types.histology: Macrovesicular steatosis + lobular inflammation + hepatocyte ballooning ± pericellular fibrosis ± Mallory-Denk bodies (ubiquitinated keratin aggregates)
types.nas_score: NASH Activity Score (NAS): steatosis (0-3) + lobular inflammation (0-3) + ballooning (0-2) = max 8; NAS ≥5 = definite NASH; NAS ≤2 = not NASH
types.prevalence: ~20-30% of NAFLD patients have NASH; ~25-37% of NASH patients will develop advanced fibrosis over 5-15 years
types.risk_of_progression: Annual progression rate from NASH to cirrhosis: ~2-3% per year; HCC can occur even in non-cirrhotic NASH (unusual for other causes)
types.management: Intensive lifestyle modification; weight loss ≥7-10%; FDA-approved resmetirom (2024); pioglitazone in diabetes; Vitamin E in non-diabetics; surgical evaluation for weight loss surgery in obese patients; clinical trial enrolment

types.name: Alcoholic Fatty Liver (AFL)
types.description: Fat accumulation in the liver from chronic excessive alcohol consumption. The earliest stage of alcoholic liver disease (ALD). Occurs in up to 90% of heavy drinkers. Clinically and histologically similar to non-alcoholic fatty liver but with alcohol exposure as the causative agent. Typically reversible with alcohol abstinence (within 4-6 weeks).
types.alcohol_threshold: Significant alcohol consumption: >14 units/week women; >21 units/week men (WHO); some guidelines: >10g/day women; >20g/day men
types.histology: Macrovesicular steatosis; centrilobular predominance (zone 3); may have perivenular fibrosis
types.reversibility: Highly reversible with complete alcohol abstinence within 4-8 weeks
types.management: Alcohol abstinence is the single most important intervention; nutritional support; thiamine supplementation

types.name: Alcoholic Hepatitis (AH)
types.description: An acute inflammatory syndrome superimposed on chronic alcoholic liver disease — often precipitated by continued heavy drinking. A medical emergency in severe cases. Histologically: steatosis + intense hepatocyte ballooning and injury + neutrophilic infiltration + Mallory-Denk bodies + pericellular fibrosis. Severity assessed by Maddrey's Discriminant Function (MDF) and MELD score.

severity_classification.maddrey_discriminant_function: MDF = 4.6 × (PT - control PT) + serum bilirubin (µmol/L)/17; MDF ≥32 = severe alcoholic hepatitis — treat with corticosteroids
severity_classification.lille_score: Response to corticosteroid treatment at 7 days — Lille score >0.45 = poor steroid response; consider stopping steroids; consider transplant assessment

types.mortality: Severe AH: 30-40% 90-day mortality; 30-50% 6-month mortality without treatment
types.management: Prednisolone 40mg/day × 28 days (MDF ≥32); Pentoxifylline if steroids contraindicated; nutritional support; alcohol abstinence; N-acetylcysteine adjuvant; liver transplant in carefully selected non-responders

types.name: Drug-Induced Fatty Liver Disease (DIAFLD)
types.description: Hepatic steatosis caused by medications — either directly injuring hepatocytes or promoting metabolic dysfunction causing fat accumulation. Important and often overlooked cause of elevated liver enzymes. The pattern may be micro- or macrovesicular steatosis depending on the drug.
causative_drugs: Amiodarone — microvesicular steatosis; phospholipidosis; cumulative dose-dependent toxicity
Methotrexate — fibrosis risk; requires liver monitoring (FibroScan) at cumulative doses
Tamoxifen — promotes NAFLD/NASH in breast cancer patients
Corticosteroids — promote insulin resistance and de novo lipogenesis
Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs — d4T, ddI) — mitochondrial toxicity; lactic acidosis
Glucocorticoids — weight gain and insulin resistance promoting hepatic steatosis
Tetracyclines (especially IV) — mitochondrial inhibition; microvesicular steatosis
Antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine) — weight gain and insulin resistance
types.management: Identify and discontinue causative drug where possible; switch to alternative; supportive liver care

types.name: Fibrotic NAFLD/MASLD (Advanced Fibrosis — F2-F4)
types.description: The critical prognostic stage of NAFLD/MASLD — hepatic fibrosis is the strongest predictor of liver-related mortality and progression to cirrhosis. Fibrosis begins pericellularly (around hepatocytes and sinusoids in zone 3), progresses to periportal, then bridging fibrosis, and finally cirrhosis. Liver-related outcomes (varices, ascites, liver failure, HCC) are directly related to fibrosis stage.

fibrosis_staging.F3: Bridging fibrosis (septae connecting portal tracts — significant architectural disruption)

types.liver_stiffness_kPa: F0: <5 kPa; F1: 5-7 kPa; F2: 7-9 kPa; F3: 9-13 kPa; F4/Cirrhosis: >13-15 kPa (FibroScan values — NAFLD context)
types.significance: F3-F4 fibrosis associated with dramatically increased liver-related mortality; HCC risk increases exponentially with fibrosis stage

types.name: NAFLD/MASLD-related Cirrhosis
types.description: End-stage NASH/MASH — complete hepatic architectural disruption with regenerative nodules, portal hypertension, and progressive hepatic synthetic failure. NASH-cirrhosis is the 3rd leading cause of liver transplantation in the USA (rising to 1st projected by 2030). Once cirrhosis is established, NASH activity often 'burns out' — making histological diagnosis of NASH-origin cirrhosis challenging ('cryptogenic cirrhosis' in many cases has retrospective NASH aetiology).
types.management: Portal hypertension management; hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance (6-monthly ultrasound ± AFP); liver transplantation evaluation; metabolic comorbidity management

types.name: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy (AFLP)
types.description: A rare but life-threatening obstetric emergency characterised by acute microvesicular fatty infiltration of the liver developing in the 3rd trimester (weeks 30-38) or immediately postpartum. Caused by mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation defects (particularly LCHAD deficiency in mother or fetus). Presents with: jaundice, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, and renal failure.
types.incidence: Rare — 1 in 7,000-16,000 deliveries; maternal mortality 7-18%; foetal mortality up to 25% without immediate delivery
types.diagnosis: Swansea criteria (≥6 of 14 criteria including jaundice, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, elevated ammonia, renal impairment, ultrasound changes)
types.management: IMMEDIATE DELIVERY regardless of gestational age — the definitive treatment; intensive care support; coagulopathy management; hypoglycaemia correction; rarely liver transplantation; screen baby for LCHAD deficiency

severity_levels.name: Mild — Simple Steatosis (Grade 1)
severity_levels.description: Fat in 5-33% of hepatocytes; no significant inflammation or ballooning; no fibrosis
severity_levels.liver_enzymes: Normal or up to 2x ULN (ALT slightly elevated)
severity_levels.ultrasound: Mild diffuse increase in liver echogenicity
severity_levels.management: Lifestyle modification (diet + exercise); 5% weight loss target; treat metabolic risk factors; reassess at 6-12 months
severity_levels.prognosis: Excellent — reversible with lifestyle changes; low progression risk

severity_levels.name: Moderate — Steatohepatitis without Fibrosis (Grade 2-3 NASH, F0-F1)
severity_levels.description: Fat in 33-66% of hepatocytes; moderate to severe lobular inflammation; hepatocyte ballooning present; minimal or no fibrosis
severity_levels.liver_enzymes: ALT 2-5x ULN; AST commonly elevated; AST:ALT <1 in NAFLD (typically)
severity_levels.symptoms: Fatigue; RUQ discomfort; possible hepatomegaly on examination
severity_levels.management: Intensive lifestyle modification (7-10% weight loss); pharmacotherapy consideration (resmetirom, pioglitazone, Vitamin E); 6-monthly monitoring; metabolic optimisation; consider bariatric surgery if obese
severity_levels.prognosis: Moderate risk of progression; intervention can reverse or halt progression

severity_levels.name: Severe — NASH with Significant Fibrosis (F2-F3)
severity_levels.description: Active NASH with perisinusoidal and periportal fibrosis progressing to bridging fibrosis; significant risk of progression to cirrhosis
severity_levels.liver_enzymes: ALT and AST variably elevated (may normalise with 'burnt-out' NASH); thrombocytopenia (splenomegaly); INR beginning to rise
severity_levels.symptoms: Persistent fatigue; RUQ pain; splenomegaly; possible early portal hypertension signs
severity_levels.management: Specialist hepatology referral; pharmacotherapy (resmetirom for F2-F3 non-cirrhotic MASH — FDA 2024); aggressive weight loss including surgical consideration; HCC surveillance initiation if cirrhosis approached; cardiovascular risk management
severity_levels.prognosis: Significant liver-related morbidity risk; fibrosis progression variable; lifestyle intervention can still improve outcomes

severity_levels.name: Critical — NASH-Cirrhosis (F4) / Decompensated Liver Disease
severity_levels.description: Established cirrhosis ± decompensation (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, jaundice). Hepatocellular carcinoma risk significantly elevated. Liver transplantation may be the only curative option.
severity_levels.liver_enzymes: May be normal or low ALT/AST (burnt out NASH); low albumin; prolonged PT/INR; thrombocytopenia
severity_levels.MELD_score: MELD score used for transplant listing priority (score >15: consider transplant referral; >17: survival benefit from transplant)
severity_levels.symptoms: Jaundice, ascites, oedema, hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis), variceal haemorrhage, muscle wasting (sarcopenia), easy bruising
severity_levels.management: Hepatology and liver transplant centre referral; 6-monthly HCC surveillance (ultrasound ± AFP); variceal screening endoscopy; ascites management (diuretics; paracentesis); lactulose + rifaximin for encephalopathy; propranolol for portal hypertension; nutritional support; abstinence from all hepatotoxins
severity_levels.prognosis: Liver transplantation is definitive treatment; 5-year post-transplant survival >80% for NASH-cirrhosis

nafld_masld_pathogenesis.overview: NAFLD/MASLD pathogenesis is complex and multifactorial — the 'multiple parallel hits' model has replaced the older 'two-hit' hypothesis. Multiple simultaneous insults drive hepatic steatosis and inflammation.
nafld_masld_pathogenesis.hit_1_lipid_accumulation: Insulin resistance → increased lipolysis in adipose tissue → increased free fatty acids (FFA) delivery to liver → increased de novo lipogenesis (DNL) in liver → decreased fatty acid beta-oxidation → triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes
nafld_masld_pathogenesis.hit_2_inflammation: Lipotoxicity (toxic effects of FFA and ceramides); oxidative stress (mitochondrial dysfunction, ER stress, reactive oxygen species); gut dysbiosis (increased intestinal permeability, bacterial products including LPS activating hepatic Kupffer cells via TLR4); adipokine dysregulation (increased TNF-α, IL-6, leptin; decreased adiponectin)
nafld_masld_pathogenesis.hit_3_fibrogenesis: Hepatocyte injury and death activates hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) → myofibroblast differentiation → excess collagen production → fibrosis → cirrhosis
nafld_masld_pathogenesis.gut_liver_axis: Dysbiosis of gut microbiome (reduced Bacteroidetes, increased Firmicutes and Proteobacteria) increases intestinal permeability and bacterial endotoxin (LPS) translocation to portal circulation → activates Kupffer cells → pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β) → liver injury

alcoholic_ld_pathogenesis.primary_mechanism: Alcohol (ethanol) is metabolised in hepatocytes to acetaldehyde (by alcohol dehydrogenase — ADH) then acetate (by aldehyde dehydrogenase — ALDH). Both pathways alter NADH:NAD+ ratio → impairs fatty acid beta-oxidation → fat accumulation. Acetaldehyde forms protein and DNA adducts causing direct hepatocyte injury.
secondary_mechanisms: Acetaldehyde protein adducts activate immune response (Kupffer cells, T-cells)
Gut dysbiosis and leaky gut (alcohol disrupts intestinal tight junctions)
Endotoxin (LPS) from gut bacteria activates TLR4 on Kupffer cells
Oxidative stress (CYP2E1 induction — produces reactive oxygen species)
alcoholic_ld_pathogenesis.genetic_factors: ALDH2 deficiency (common in East Asians — 'Asian Flush') causes acetaldehyde accumulation; ADH1B variants affect alcohol metabolism rate

genetic_factors_nafld.effect: Most important genetic determinant of NAFLD. Encodes patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing protein 3 involved in lipid metabolism. I148M variant (G→A mutation) impairs VLDL secretion and increases de novo lipogenesis. 2-3x increased NASH and cirrhosis risk. Higher frequency in Hispanics (explaining higher NAFLD prevalence).
genetic_factors_nafld.prevalence: G allele frequency: Hispanics 49%, Europeans 23%, Africans 17%

genetic_factors_nafld.effect: Transmembrane 6 superfamily member 2 — regulates VLDL secretion. Loss-of-function variant reduces VLDL secretion → triglyceride retention in hepatocytes → increased NASH/fibrosis risk; paradoxically lower cardiovascular risk (reduced VLDL/LDL)
Membrane-bound O-acyltransferase domain-containing 7 — regulates phospholipid remodelling. Risk variant associated with more severe NAFLD and cirrhosis
Glucokinase regulatory protein — regulates glucose metabolism. Variant promotes de novo lipogenesis from excess glucose; higher NAFLD and NASH risk

risk_factors_nafld_masld.evidence: Strongest risk factor — NAFLD prevalence: 60-90% in severely obese (BMI >35); 30-50% in overweight (BMI 25-30); 3-5% in lean individuals. Central adiposity (visceral fat) more important than total obesity. Each 5-unit BMI increase raises NAFLD odds by 3.5x.
risk_factors_nafld_masld.mechanism: Excess visceral adipose tissue releases FFAs and pro-inflammatory adipokines (TNF-α, IL-6, leptin); insulin resistance

risk_factors_nafld_masld.evidence: NAFLD prevalence ~70% in T2DM; diabetics have 2-3x higher risk of advanced fibrosis and HCC. NAFLD and T2DM bidirectionally worsen each other.
risk_factors_nafld_masld.mechanism: Hyperinsulinaemia promotes hepatic de novo lipogenesis; insulin resistance impairs hepatic fatty acid oxidation

risk_factors_nafld_masld.evidence: Each component of metabolic syndrome independently increases NAFLD risk; presence of full metabolic syndrome (central obesity + diabetes/impaired glucose + hypertriglyceridaemia + low HDL + hypertension) carries 5-6x NAFLD risk
risk_factors_nafld_masld.mechanism: Insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, and inflammatory state drive hepatic steatosis

risk_factors_nafld_masld.evidence: Hypertriglyceridaemia strongly associated with NAFLD; high serum triglycerides reflect excess hepatic VLDL production
risk_factors_nafld_masld.mechanism: Elevated serum FFAs from hypertriglyceridaemia → hepatic triglyceride influx

risk_factors_nafld_masld.evidence: Hypothyroidism is an independent risk factor for NAFLD and NASH; thyroid hormone (T3) promotes hepatic fatty acid oxidation — deficiency impairs this
risk_factors_nafld_masld.action: Always check TSH in patients with unexplained fatty liver

risk_factors_nafld_masld.evidence: NAFLD prevalence 30-70% in PCOS; driven by insulin resistance, hyperandrogenism, and metabolic syndrome features
risk_factors_nafld_masld.note: NAFLD in young women with PCOS is increasingly recognised — screen with liver ultrasound

risk_factors_nafld_masld.evidence: OSA independently associated with NAFLD and NASH (beyond shared obesity risk); intermittent hypoxia during apnoeas promotes oxidative stress and hepatic steatohepatitis
risk_factors_nafld_masld.note: CPAP therapy for OSA may modestly improve liver function

risk_factors_ald: Daily alcohol consumption (dose-dependent): >14 units/week women; >21 units/week men significantly increases risk
Drinking pattern: binge drinking more harmful than the same total dose consumed steadily
Female sex: women develop liver disease at lower alcohol doses and faster than men (lower first-pass metabolism, lower body water content)
Genetic factors: ALDH2*2 allele (East Asian); PNPLA3 I148M; HSD17B13 variants modulate ALD risk
Nutritional status: malnutrition worsens ALD severity
Obesity co-existing with alcohol: synergistic hepatotoxicity — combined risk is multiplicative, not additive
Concomitant HCV or HBV infection: dramatically accelerates ALD progression
Iron overload (haemochromatosis) co-exiting with ALD: accelerated fibrosis

symptoms.important_note: Fatty liver disease — particularly in its early stages (simple steatosis and even early NASH) — is characteristically ASYMPTOMATIC. The majority of patients are diagnosed incidentally through abnormal liver function tests on routine blood tests, or abnormal hepatic echogenicity on abdominal ultrasound performed for other reasons. The absence of symptoms does NOT mean the disease is not progressing.

primary_symptoms.name: Fatigue and Lethargy
primary_symptoms.description: The most common symptom of fatty liver disease — present in 50-75% of patients with NAFLD/NASH. A non-specific symptom that significantly impairs quality of life. Mechanisms include: mitochondrial dysfunction in hepatocytes (reduces energy production); inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6 causing 'sickness behaviour'); sleep disturbance from associated sleep apnoea; anaemia from chronic liver disease; psychological impact of chronic illness. Fatigue in NASH does not reliably correlate with liver enzyme elevation or histological severity.
primary_symptoms.note: Disproportionate fatigue out of context with other findings should trigger liver function testing

primary_symptoms.name: Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ) Discomfort or Dull Ache
primary_symptoms.description: A vague, dull, non-specific ache or heaviness in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen — the anatomical location of the liver. Results from stretching of the liver capsule (Glisson's capsule) as the liver enlarges (hepatomegaly) from fat accumulation. Not typically sharp or severe — sharp or severe pain should prompt investigation for other causes (cholelithiasis, biliary colic, right-sided pleurisy).
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual; may worsen after large meals (post-prandial hepatic blood flow increase)

primary_symptoms.name: Hepatomegaly (Enlarged Liver)
primary_symptoms.description: Enlargement of the liver due to fat accumulation — palpable below the right costal margin on abdominal examination (normally the liver is not palpable). Present in 50-75% of patients with NAFLD on careful examination. Confirmed on ultrasound or CT. May produce a dull ache. The degree of hepatomegaly does not reliably correlate with disease severity.
primary_symptoms.clinical_finding: Liver palpable >2cm below right costal margin; smooth liver edge (in NAFLD; irregular nodular in cirrhosis)

primary_symptoms.name: Symptoms of Metabolic Syndrome (Co-existing)
primary_symptoms.description: Most patients with NAFLD/MASLD have visible and symptomatic features of their underlying metabolic condition: central obesity (abdominal weight gain, large waist circumference), excessive thirst and urination (diabetes), hypertension headaches, and fatigue from insulin resistance. The metabolic features are often more prominent than liver-specific symptoms.
primary_symptoms.note: Presence of metabolic features (obesity, T2DM, dyslipidaemia, hypertension) in a patient with any liver abnormality should prompt NAFLD screening

primary_symptoms.name: Jaundice (in Advanced Disease)
primary_symptoms.description: Yellowing of the skin, sclerae (whites of eyes), and mucous membranes from elevated serum bilirubin (>35 µmol/L causes visible jaundice). NOT a feature of simple steatosis or early NASH. Occurs with: severe alcoholic hepatitis (acute onset jaundice + tender hepatomegaly + fever after heavy drinking); decompensated NASH-cirrhosis; acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Jaundice in a patient with known fatty liver disease is an ALARM SIGN requiring urgent evaluation.
primary_symptoms.onset: Acute (alcoholic hepatitis, AFLP) or gradual (decompensating cirrhosis)

primary_symptoms.name: Signs of Portal Hypertension and Cirrhosis (Late Stage)
primary_symptoms.description: As NASH progresses to cirrhosis, portal hypertension develops — elevated pressure in the portal venous system from fibrotic obstruction of hepatic blood flow. Clinical features: splenomegaly (enlarged spleen — palpable in left flank); ascites (fluid accumulation in abdominal cavity — distended abdomen, shifting dullness on percussion, fluid thrill); caput medusae (dilated periumbilical veins); peripheral oedema.
primary_symptoms.severity: Severe — indicates advanced cirrhosis and portal hypertension
specific_signs: Ascites — fluid wave, shifting dullness on percussion
Splenomegaly — palpable left flank mass; thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism
Caput medusae — dilated veins radiating from umbilicus
Spider naevi — cutaneous arteriovenous shunts; >5 significant; upper body and face
Gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy (men) — from oestrogen excess in liver failure

secondary_symptoms: Nausea and reduced appetite — hepatic inflammation; elevated cytokines; gastroparesis (in diabetic NAFLD)
Weight gain — associated metabolic syndrome; rarely paradoxical weight loss in advanced cirrhosis (muscle wasting/cachexia)
Headache — associated hypertension (metabolic syndrome) or sleep apnoea
Snoring and witnessed apnoeas — obstructive sleep apnoea (very common comorbidity in NAFLD — 30-50%)
Excessive sweating and skin darkening — acanthosis nigricans (dark velvety skin in neck, axillae — sign of severe insulin resistance)
Joint pain — hyperuricaemia/gout (associated with metabolic syndrome and fructose-rich diet)
Peripheral neuropathy — in T2DM with NAFLD
Erectile dysfunction — from metabolic syndrome and vascular disease
Easy bruising — early sign of reduced hepatic clotting factor synthesis in advanced disease
Confusion and cognitive impairment — hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis (ammonia accumulation; Grade I-IV)
Pruritus (itching) — in cholestatic variants; with bile acid accumulation
Haematemesis (vomiting blood) — variceal bleeding in portal hypertension — EMERGENCY
symptoms_specific_to_alcoholic_hepatitis: Acute onset jaundice after heavy alcohol binge (characteristic presentation)
Severe right upper quadrant pain and tender hepatomegaly
High fever (bacterial infection common — must rule out SBP)
Signs of coagulopathy — easy bruising, petechiae
warning_signs: Jaundice appearing or worsening rapidly — URGENT evaluation
Haematemesis (vomiting blood) or melaena — variceal bleeding emergency — CALL 999/112/102
Sudden-onset confusion, disorientation, or loss of consciousness — hepatic encephalopathy emergency
Abdominal pain, fever, and ascites — spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) — life-threatening emergency
Rapid ascites development with increasing abdominal girth
Progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools in pregnancy (3rd trimester) — AFLP — obstetric emergency
Significant unintentional weight loss in a patient with NAFLD — possible hepatocellular carcinoma

diagnostic_approach.overview: Fatty liver disease diagnosis involves three levels: (1) Detection of hepatic steatosis (ultrasound, CT, MRI, or liver biopsy); (2) Assessment of inflammation and injury (liver function tests, biopsy); (3) Assessment of fibrosis stage (non-invasive — FibroScan, FIB-4, APRI; or invasive — liver biopsy). Liver biopsy remains the gold standard but is invasive — non-invasive tools are now widely used and recommended by guidelines for initial evaluation.
diagnostic_approach.step_1_detection: Abnormal liver enzymes (ALT/AST) or incidental ultrasound finding → confirm hepatic steatosis
diagnostic_approach.step_2_aetiology: Exclude other causes: viral hepatitis (HBsAg, anti-HCV), autoimmune (ANA, SMA, IgG), genetic (ferritin, transferrin saturation for haemochromatosis; caeruloplasmin for Wilson's), alcoholic (alcohol history, AST:ALT ratio, GGT), drug-induced
diagnostic_approach.step_3_fibrosis: Non-invasive fibrosis assessment (FIB-4, NFS, FibroScan); liver biopsy if non-invasive tests indeterminate or conflicting

medical_history: Alcohol history: detailed quantification of alcohol consumption (type, volume, frequency, duration); AUDIT questionnaire; pattern of drinking (daily vs binge); abstinence periods
Metabolic history: obesity (BMI history, weight gain timeline), diabetes (type, duration, control — HbA1c), dyslipidaemia (cholesterol, triglycerides), hypertension, metabolic syndrome features

Medication history: all current and recent medications especially hepatotoxic drugs (amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen, corticosteroids, valproate, antiretrovirals); OTC supplements and herbal medicines
Family history: liver disease, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, haemochromatosis, Wilson's disease
Dietary history: fructose and sugar-sweetened beverage consumption, high-fat diet, ultra-processed food intake; coffee consumption (hepatoprotective)
Occupational history: chemical or solvent exposure (hepatotoxins)
Previous liver investigations: prior liver function tests, liver ultrasound results
Symptom history: fatigue severity, RUQ pain, jaundice history, abdominal swelling
Pregnancy history: AFLP in previous pregnancies; LCHAD deficiency history
Bariatric surgery history: weight loss surgery can worsen or improve NAFLD depending on type
physical_examination: BMI calculation and waist circumference measurement — central obesity assessment

Abdominal examination: liver size (percuss and palpate for hepatomegaly — >2cm below right costal margin); liver texture (smooth = steatosis; nodular = cirrhosis); spleen size (splenomegaly — portal hypertension); ascites (shifting dullness, fluid thrill)

Signs of chronic liver disease: spider naevi (upper body), palmar erythema, leuconychia (white nails), Dupuytren's contracture (ALD), gynaecomastia (men), testicular atrophy (men), parotid enlargement (ALD), Dupuytren's
Signs of portal hypertension: caput medusae (periumbilical vein dilation); ascites; splenomegaly; peripheral oedema
Neurological: asterixis (flapping tremor of hands — hepatic encephalopathy — ask patient to hold arms outstretched and dorsiflex wrists; flapping indicates encephalopathy)
Skin examination: acanthosis nigricans (thick dark velvety skin at neck, axillae — insulin resistance); jaundice; scratch marks (pruritus from cholestasis)
Eyes: scleral icterus (jaundice); Kayser-Fleischer rings (Wilson's disease — seen at slit-lamp only)
Cardiovascular: signs of heart failure (oedema, raised JVP) — cardiac cause of hepatic congestion excluded

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Liver Function Tests (LFTs) — Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT), Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)
diagnostic_tests.description: The most common initial abnormality leading to NAFLD diagnosis. ALT is more liver-specific than AST. In NAFLD: ALT is usually mildly elevated (1-4x upper limit of normal — ULN); AST:ALT ratio typically <1 (liver-predominant ALT elevation). In ALD: AST:ALT ratio >2:1 is characteristic (alcohol preferentially affects mitochondria — elevates AST; also alcohol depletes hepatic pyridoxal phosphate required for ALT synthesis). Normal LFTs do NOT exclude NAFLD or NASH — 20-30% of NASH patients have persistently normal LFTs.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Initial assessment of liver injury; monitor disease progression; assess treatment response
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ALT >ULN in context of metabolic risk factors = NAFLD until excluded; AST:ALT >2:1 = suggests ALD; ALT >10x ULN or rapidly rising = acute liver injury — urgent investigation

diagnostic_tests.description: GGT: elevated in NAFLD, ALD, and cholestasis; GGT rise is particularly sensitive for alcohol consumption (rises within days of alcohol use — useful clinical marker of recent drinking); GGT is a cardiovascular risk marker in NAFLD. ALP: elevated in cholestatic conditions; mild elevation in NAFLD. Bilirubin: usually normal in simple steatosis/early NASH; elevated in alcoholic hepatitis and decompensated cirrhosis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess cholestasis; GGT as alcohol sensitivity marker; disease severity assessment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: GGT >3x ULN with raised AST and alcohol history: strongly suggests ALD; disproportionate ALP elevation: investigate cholestatic cause (primary biliary cholangitis — AMA antibody)

diagnostic_tests.description: Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) is an early sign of portal hypertension and hypersplenism from advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis. Anaemia may be present (chronic disease, iron deficiency, haemolysis in Wilson's, macrocytic from alcohol/folate deficiency). Raised WBC in alcoholic hepatitis or SBP.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect thrombocytopenia (portal hypertension — advanced fibrosis marker); anaemia assessment; infection screen
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Platelets <150,000/µL: suggests portal hypertension and F3-F4 fibrosis; Platelets <100,000: significant portal hypertension; Macrocytic anaemia: alcohol or B12/folate deficiency

diagnostic_tests.description: Insulin resistance is central to NAFLD pathogenesis. HbA1c provides 3-month average glucose control. HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance) = fasting glucose (mmol/L) × fasting insulin (mU/L) ÷ 22.5; HOMA-IR >2.5 indicates insulin resistance.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess insulin resistance (core pathophysiological mechanism); diagnose diabetes/prediabetes; guide pharmacotherapy decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) = diabetes; 42-47 mmol/mol = prediabetes (high NASH risk); HOMA-IR >2.5 = insulin resistance

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Fasting Lipid Profile (Triglycerides, LDL, HDL, Total Cholesterol)
diagnostic_tests.description: Dyslipidaemia is extremely common in NAFLD — particularly hypertriglyceridaemia (excess hepatic VLDL production) and low HDL. Elevated LDL/ApoB in metabolic NAFLD. Cardiovascular disease is the primary cause of death in NAFLD (more common than liver-related mortality in early NAFLD) — lipid management is critical.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess cardiovascular risk (primary cause of death in NAFLD); identify dyslipidaemia (MASLD diagnostic criterion); guide statin therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L): MASLD diagnostic criterion; HDL <40 (men) or <50 (women) mg/dL: MASLD criterion; LDL >3.0 mmol/L: treat with statin

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Viral Hepatitis Screen (HBsAg, Anti-HCV, HBeAg, HBV-DNA)
diagnostic_tests.description: Viral hepatitis (HBV and HCV) must be excluded as a cause of liver disease and can coexist with NAFLD. HCV in particular causes hepatic steatosis (especially genotype 3 — direct steatogenic effect). HBV coexisting with NAFLD accelerates fibrosis. Mandatory exclusion in all patients with liver disease.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude HBV and HCV as cause or contributor to liver disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: HBsAg positive: active HBV infection; Anti-HCV positive: past or current HCV infection (confirm with HCV-RNA PCR)

diagnostic_tests.description: Hypothyroidism is an independent risk factor for NAFLD (thyroid hormone T3 stimulates hepatic fatty acid beta-oxidation — deficiency impairs fat clearance). Thyroid screening is recommended in all NAFLD patients. Hypothyroidism treatment may modestly improve NAFLD.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for hypothyroidism as secondary cause of NAFLD
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TSH >4 mIU/L: hypothyroidism — treat and reassess liver function

diagnostic_tests.description: Screen for haemochromatosis (hereditary iron overload — HFE C282Y/H63D mutations) as a cause of liver disease. Ferritin is also elevated in NAFLD/NASH as an acute phase reactant (metabolic hyperferritinaemia) — does NOT always indicate iron overload. Transferrin saturation >45% warrants HFE gene testing.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for haemochromatosis (secondary cause of fatty liver); assess iron overload
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Ferritin >300 (men) or >200 (women) µg/L + transferrin saturation >45%: investigate haemochromatosis (HFE gene testing); elevated ferritin with normal transferrin saturation: inflammatory (metabolic hyperferritinaemia)

diagnostic_tests.description: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) can cause fatty liver changes and elevated liver enzymes — must be excluded especially in women under 40. ANA (antinuclear antibody), SMA (smooth muscle antibody), and anti-LKM1 + elevated IgG are hallmarks of AIH.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude autoimmune hepatitis as a cause of liver disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ANA or SMA >1:80 + elevated IgG: suggests autoimmune hepatitis; confirm with liver biopsy

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Caeruloplasmin and 24-hour Urine Copper (Wilson's Disease)
diagnostic_tests.description: Wilson's disease (autosomal recessive copper metabolism disorder) presents in young patients (<40 years) with liver disease, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and haemolytic anaemia. Should be excluded in any young patient with unexplained liver disease or fatty liver.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude Wilson's disease in patients <40 years with unexplained liver disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Caeruloplasmin <0.2 g/L (low) + 24h urine copper >100 µg/day: Wilson's disease; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination

diagnostic_tests.description: First-line imaging for fatty liver disease — safe (no radiation), widely available, inexpensive. Detects hepatic steatosis as increased liver echogenicity (hyperechoic, 'bright liver') compared to renal cortex. Also assesses liver size, spleen size (splenomegaly → portal hypertension), ascites, biliary system, and portal vein.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect and grade steatosis; assess liver size; detect splenomegaly and ascites; assess portal vein; exclude biliary disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Increased hepatic echogenicity compared to renal cortex = steatosis; poor visualisation of diaphragm and hepatic veins = moderate-severe steatosis; nodular irregular liver edge = cirrhosis; splenomegaly = portal hypertension
diagnostic_tests.sensitivity: Sensitivity for steatosis >30%: 85-90%; for steatosis <30%: lower (~50%); cannot reliably detect fibrosis or NASH
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Cannot grade fibrosis; cannot detect NASH (inflammation); less sensitive for mild steatosis; operator-dependent

diagnostic_tests.description: Non-invasive point-of-care test combining transient elastography (measures liver stiffness — correlates with fibrosis stage) and Controlled Attenuation Parameter (CAP — measures hepatic steatosis grade). A brief, painless, 10-minute procedure performed in clinic. The most important non-invasive test for fibrosis staging in NAFLD. Liver stiffness measurement (LSM) in kilopascals (kPa) correlates with fibrosis stage.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Non-invasive fibrosis staging (most important clinical application); steatosis grading via CAP; monitoring treatment response; screening for significant fibrosis
diagnostic_tests.liver_stiffness_NAFLD: F0-F1: <7.0 kPa; F2: 7-9 kPa; F3: 9-13 kPa; F4/Cirrhosis: >13-15 kPa (EASL 2016 cut-offs for NAFLD — varies by guideline and aetiology)
diagnostic_tests.limitations: BMI >40 or intercostal space <25mm reduces accuracy (use XL probe); unreliable in acute hepatitis (inflammation falsely raises stiffness); must fast for 2 hours before test; avoid after exercise (false elevation)
diagnostic_tests.advantage: Painless; 10-minute clinic procedure; immediate results; no radiation; reproducible

diagnostic_tests.description: A simple validated non-invasive fibrosis score calculated from age, AST, ALT, and platelet count. Recommended by NICE (UK) and EASL (Europe) as the first-line non-invasive fibrosis risk stratification tool in primary care before FibroScan. Can be calculated online or from laboratory results instantly.
diagnostic_tests.interpretation: <1.30: Low risk of advanced fibrosis (F0-F2 — reassure, lifestyle advice, 3-yearly review); 1.30-2.67: Indeterminate — FibroScan required; >2.67: High risk of advanced fibrosis (F3-F4) — urgent hepatology referral
diagnostic_tests.sensitivity_specificity: Sensitivity ~70%, Specificity ~80% for advanced fibrosis (F3-F4); validated in large NAFLD cohorts
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Primary care stratification of NAFLD patients; decide who needs FibroScan or hepatology referral; most cost-effective initial non-invasive test

diagnostic_tests.description: Another validated non-invasive fibrosis score using: age, BMI, impaired fasting glucose/diabetes status, AST:ALT ratio, platelets, and albumin.
diagnostic_tests.formula: NFS = -1.675 + 0.037 × age + 0.094 × BMI + 1.13 × IFG/diabetes (yes=1, no=0) + 0.99 × AST/ALT ratio − 0.013 × platelets − 0.66 × albumin
diagnostic_tests.interpretation: NFS < −1.455: F0-F2 (low fibrosis risk); NFS −1.455 to 0.676: indeterminate; NFS >0.676: F3-F4 (high fibrosis risk)
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Alternative non-invasive fibrosis stratification; comparable accuracy to FIB-4

diagnostic_tests.test_name: MRI Proton Density Fat Fraction (MRI-PDFF) and MR Elastography (MRE)
diagnostic_tests.description: The gold standard non-invasive tests for fat quantification and fibrosis assessment respectively. MRI-PDFF accurately quantifies hepatic fat content (superior to ultrasound and CT). MR Elastography measures liver stiffness via propagated shear waves — superior to FibroScan for fibrosis staging especially in obese patients. Not universally available — specialist centres.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: MRI-PDFF: accurate fat quantification (clinical trials endpoint); monitor response to therapy. MRE: superior non-invasive fibrosis staging; useful when FibroScan technically limited (morbid obesity)
diagnostic_tests.advantage: No radiation; excellent accuracy; MRE superior to FibroScan in obese patients
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Expensive; time-consuming; not universally available; contraindicated with some implants

diagnostic_tests.description: The definitive diagnostic test — remains the gold standard for grading steatosis, inflammation, and hepatocyte ballooning (NASH diagnosis) and staging fibrosis. Provides the NAS (NAFLD Activity Score) and fibrosis stage (F0-F4). Guided by ultrasound or CT. Transjugular approach when coagulopathy present.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Definitive NASH diagnosis; accurate fibrosis staging when non-invasive tests are discordant; before antifibrotic therapy; clinical trial enrolment; unexplained liver disease
diagnostic_tests.histological_features_NASH: Steatosis (macrovesicular, acinar zone 3 predominant); lobular inflammation (neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltration); hepatocyte ballooning (swollen pale hepatocytes — pathognomonic for NASH); pericellular fibrosis (zone 3, 'chicken wire' pattern); Mallory-Denk bodies (eosinophilic keratin aggregates in ballooned hepatocytes)
diagnostic_tests.risks: Bleeding (1 in 500-1000); pain; rare perforation; death (<1 in 10,000)
diagnostic_tests.indications: Non-invasive tests discordant; before pharmacotherapy requiring biopsy-proven NASH (resmetirom indication is biopsy-confirmed); unexplained liver disease; clinical trial requirement; assessment of other coexisting liver pathology

diagnostic_tests.description: Six-monthly HCC surveillance ultrasound ± AFP is recommended for all patients with NASH-cirrhosis (F4). HCC can also arise in non-cirrhotic NASH (unique — most other liver cancer aetiologies require cirrhosis) — surveillance protocol for non-cirrhotic NASH with F3 fibrosis is evolving.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) — early-stage HCC has curative treatment options; late-stage detection has poor prognosis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: AFP >20 ng/mL + liver lesion on ultrasound: urgent CT/MRI for HCC characterisation; AFP >400 ng/mL: HCC until proven otherwise

diagnostic_tests.description: Screening for oesophageal and gastric varices — dilated veins from portal hypertension that can rupture causing potentially fatal haemorrhage. Recommended in all patients with newly diagnosed cirrhosis and all patients with signs of portal hypertension (splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Variceal screening; primary prophylaxis with beta-blocker (propranolol/carvedilol) or band ligation for medium-large varices
diagnostic_tests.frequency: At cirrhosis diagnosis: if no varices — repeat every 2-3 years; if small varices — every 1-2 years; medium-large varices — prophylactic treatment

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Liver-Specific Biomarkers (ELF Score, FibroTest, VCTE + CAP)
diagnostic_tests.description: Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) Score: blood test combining HA (hyaluronic acid), PIIINP (procollagen III N-terminal peptide), and TIMP-1 — markers of active fibrogenesis. FibroTest (commercial): combines 6 blood markers with age/sex to estimate fibrosis. Used as second-line non-invasive tests when FIB-4 and FibroScan are indeterminate.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Second-line non-invasive fibrosis assessment; complement FIB-4 and FibroScan in indeterminate cases
diagnostic_tests.ELF_thresholds: ELF score <7.7: no/mild fibrosis; 7.7-9.8: moderate fibrosis; >9.8: severe fibrosis/cirrhosis

medicines.note: As of 2024, resmetirom (Rezdiffra) became the FIRST FDA-approved medication specifically for non-cirrhotic MASH with moderate-to-severe fibrosis (F2-F3). The landscape of MASH pharmacotherapy is rapidly evolving. LIFESTYLE MODIFICATION REMAINS THE MOST EFFECTIVE TREATMENT — no medication matches the efficacy of ≥7-10% sustained weight loss. All medications must be prescribed by a licensed hepatologist or gastroenterologist.
treatment_priorities: 1. Lifestyle modification: diet + exercise = most effective intervention; 7-10% weight loss reduces NASH histologically
2. Management of metabolic comorbidities: treat T2DM, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, obesity
3. Pharmacotherapy for biopsy-proven MASH F2-F3: resmetirom (2024); pioglitazone; Vitamin E
4. Bariatric surgery: for obese patients with NAFLD/MASH — most effective weight loss intervention
5. Transplantation: for end-stage NASH-cirrhosis meeting criteria

categories.category_name: Thyroid Hormone Receptor Beta Agonist — FDA-Approved for MASH (2024)
categories.purpose: Resmetirom is the first and currently only FDA-approved treatment specifically targeting MASH resolution and fibrosis improvement.

medicines.name: Resmetirom
medicines.dosage: 80mg once daily (weight <100 kg) or 100mg once daily (weight ≥100 kg); taken with or without food
medicines.use_case: FDA APPROVED March 2024 for non-cirrhotic NASH/MASH with moderate to severe fibrosis (F2-F3); must have biopsy-confirmed non-cirrhotic MASH with F2-F3 fibrosis; used alongside diet and exercise
medicines.mechanism: Selective thyroid hormone receptor beta (THR-β) agonist. THR-β is predominantly expressed in the liver — activation stimulates hepatic fatty acid oxidation, reduces de novo lipogenesis, lowers serum LDL and triglycerides, reduces liver fat. Avoids THR-α (cardiac) effects of thyroid hormone.
medicines.pivotal_trial: MAESTRO-NASH Phase 3 trial: resmetirom achieved NASH resolution without worsening fibrosis in 25-30% vs 10% placebo; fibrosis improvement ≥1 stage in 24-26% vs 14% placebo; also significantly reduced LDL and triglycerides
contraindications: Concomitant use of strong CYP2C8 inhibitors (gemfibrozil)
medicines.monitoring: LFTs at baseline, 3 months, 6 months; repeat biopsy at 52 weeks (in trials) or FibroScan for monitoring
medicines.availability: USA (approved 2024); regulatory submissions ongoing globally; not yet approved in EU or India as of 2025

categories.category_name: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists — High-Priority Emerging and Approved Agents
categories.purpose: GLP-1 receptor agonists are transformational for both T2DM/obesity management and MASH. Semaglutide demonstrates remarkable NASH resolution in clinical trials and is widely used off-label pending formal MASH indication approval. ESSENCE Phase 3 trial (semaglutide 2.4mg weekly) results published 2023-2024 show significant MASH resolution and fibrosis improvement.

medicines.name: Semaglutide
medicines.dosage: Ozempic (T2DM): 0.25mg weekly × 4 weeks → 0.5mg weekly → 1mg weekly; Wegovy (obesity): gradual titration to 2.4mg weekly over 16-20 weeks
medicines.use_case: T2DM with NAFLD/MASH (approved for diabetes); Obesity with NAFLD (Wegovy approved for obesity); Off-label for MASH — ESSENCE trial results highly promising; cardiovascular risk reduction in T2DM with liver disease
medicines.mechanism: GLP-1 receptor agonist — stimulates insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, reduces appetite, slows gastric emptying, promotes weight loss. Liver-specific effects: reduces hepatic de novo lipogenesis, reduces hepatic fat, anti-inflammatory (reduces Kupffer cell activation), reduces hepatocyte apoptosis
medicines.nash_evidence: NASH Phase 2 trial (semaglutide 0.4mg daily): NASH resolution in 59% vs 17% placebo (no significant fibrosis improvement). ESSENCE Phase 3 trial (2.4mg weekly): MASH resolution 63% vs 34% placebo; fibrosis improvement 37% vs 22% placebo — very significant; expected FDA filing for MASH indication 2024-2025
side_effects: Nausea and vomiting (dose-related — typically resolves at steady dose)
Thyroid C-cell tumours (rodent studies; contraindicated with MEN2 or medullary thyroid cancer history)
medicines.weight_loss: Semaglutide 2.4mg weekly: average 15-16% body weight reduction (STEP trials) — most of MASH benefit may be mediated through weight loss

medicines.name: Tirzepatide
medicines.dosage: 2.5mg weekly escalating to 5, 10, or 15mg weekly over months
medicines.use_case: T2DM with NAFLD; Obesity with NAFLD; MASH SYNERGY trial (Phase 3 for MASH) ongoing — highly anticipated
medicines.mechanism: Dual GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) + GLP-1 receptor agonist; superior weight loss to semaglutide; SURMOUNT trials: 20-22% weight loss
medicines.nash_evidence: SURPASS and SURMOUNT trials demonstrated significant hepatic fat reduction; SYNERGY-NASH Phase 3 trial (tirzepatide for MASH) — results expected 2024-2025
medicines.side_effects: Similar to semaglutide — nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; generally well tolerated; dose-dependent

medicines.name: Liraglutide
medicines.dosage: T2DM: 0.6mg → 1.2 → 1.8mg once daily; Obesity: 0.6mg → 3.0mg once daily over 5 weeks
medicines.use_case: T2DM with NAFLD (approved for T2DM); Obesity with NAFLD (Saxenda); less preferred than once-weekly semaglutide but evidence-based
medicines.nash_evidence: LEAN trial: liraglutide 1.8mg daily — NASH resolution 39% vs 9% placebo; fibrosis improvement 26% vs 9% placebo (Phase 2)
medicines.side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, injection site reactions; less commonly pancreatitis

categories.purpose: Reduce hepatic and peripheral insulin resistance through PPAR-gamma activation. Currently the most evidence-based pharmacological treatment for biopsy-proven NASH in diabetic patients per AASLD and EASL guidelines.

medicines.name: Pioglitazone
medicines.dosage: 15-30mg once daily (NASH: 30-45mg; diabetes: 15-30mg); monitor LFTs
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE recommended pharmacotherapy for NASH in DIABETIC adults (AASLD/EASL guidelines); biopsy-proven NASH with or without diabetes; significant evidence base from multiple RCTs
medicines.mechanism: PPAR-gamma nuclear receptor agonist — reduces hepatic and adipose insulin resistance; redirects FFAs from liver to peripheral adipose; reduces hepatic de novo lipogenesis; anti-inflammatory (reduces TNF-α, IL-6); activates adiponectin
medicines.nash_evidence: PIVENS trial (pioglitazone 30mg vs Vitamin E vs placebo in non-diabetic NASH): pioglitazone achieved NASH resolution in 34%; ACTiVST trial in T2DM NASH: significant NAS score reduction and fibrosis improvement
side_effects: Weight gain (average +3-5 kg — fluid retention and adipogenesis)
Increased risk of heart failure — CONTRAINDICATED in heart failure (Class III-IV NYHA)
Increased fracture risk (especially in women — vertebral, hip, distal arm)
Possible increased bladder cancer risk (controversial — FDA warning; avoid if prior bladder cancer)
contraindications: Heart failure (NYHA Class I-IV — significant cardiac risk)

categories.purpose: Reduces hepatic oxidative stress — a key driver of NASH progression. Recommended by AASLD for non-diabetic, non-cirrhotic adults with biopsy-proven NASH.

medicines.name: Vitamin E (Alpha-Tocopherol)
medicines.dosage: 800 IU per day (alpha-tocopherol — natural form: RRR-alpha-tocopherol preferred)
medicines.use_case: Biopsy-proven NASH WITHOUT diabetes and WITHOUT cirrhosis (per AASLD guidelines); antioxidant therapy for NASH
medicines.mechanism: Potent fat-soluble antioxidant — scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS); reduces hepatic lipid peroxidation; reduces NF-κB activation; anti-inflammatory
medicines.nash_evidence: PIVENS trial: Vitamin E 800 IU/day achieved primary endpoint (NAS improvement ≥2 points, no worsening fibrosis) in 43% vs 19% placebo; NASH resolution in 36% vs 21%; fibrosis improvement NS (no significant improvement)
side_effects: Higher doses (>400 IU/day): possible increased all-cause mortality in meta-analyses (controversial — cardiac mortality signal in SELECT trial at 400 IU/day)
Increased haemorrhagic stroke risk at very high doses
contraindications: Diabetes mellitus (pioglitazone preferred in diabetics with NASH — Vitamin E less effective)
medicines.monitoring: No specific liver monitoring required; baseline and periodic haematology if on anticoagulants
medicines.note: 400-800 IU natural Vitamin E is widely available OTC; higher doses in NASH should be under medical supervision

categories.purpose: Pan-PPAR and dual PPAR agonists target multiple metabolic pathways simultaneously — lipid metabolism, insulin resistance, and inflammation.

medicines.name: Saroglitazar (PPAR alpha/gamma dual agonist)
medicines.dosage: 4mg once daily before breakfast
medicines.use_case: Approved in India for NAFLD/NASH (CDSCO approved 2020 — first NAFLD-specific drug approved in India); T2DM with dyslipidaemia; diabetic dyslipidaemia
medicines.mechanism: Dual PPAR alpha/gamma agonist — PPAR-alpha: reduces triglycerides and hepatic lipogenesis (fibrate-like); PPAR-gamma: improves insulin sensitivity (TZD-like); combined effect addresses both steatosis and insulin resistance
medicines.nash_evidence: NAFLD trial in India: saroglitazar 4mg reduced ALT, liver fat (MRI), and improved NAS score vs placebo; approved on basis of Indian Phase 3 data
medicines.availability: India, Middle East — not yet approved in USA/EU; widely prescribed in India for NAFLD

medicines.name: Lanifibranor (Pan-PPAR agonist — PPAR alpha/gamma/delta)
medicines.dosage: 800mg or 1200mg once daily (clinical trial doses)
medicines.use_case: Phase 3 NATiV3 trial COMPLETED (2023): significant MASH resolution and fibrosis improvement; regulatory filing anticipated 2024-2025
medicines.mechanism: Pan-PPAR agonist — simultaneously targets all three PPAR receptors: alpha (lipid metabolism), gamma (insulin resistance), delta (mitochondrial biogenesis, anti-inflammatory)
medicines.nash_evidence: NATiV3 Phase 3: lanifibranor 1200mg — MASH resolution in 49% vs 22% placebo; fibrosis improvement ≥1 stage in 48% vs 29% placebo — impressive dual endpoint achievement
medicines.availability: Not yet approved; anticipated EMA and FDA filing 2024-2025

categories.category_name: Statins — Cardiovascular Risk Reduction in NAFLD
categories.purpose: Statins are SAFE in NAFLD and NASH (contrary to historical concerns) and are ESSENTIAL for cardiovascular risk reduction — cardiovascular disease is the PRIMARY cause of death in NAFLD, not liver disease. Statins may have modest anti-inflammatory hepatic benefits.
categories.note: CRITICAL POINT: Many NAFLD patients are not prescribed statins due to fear of hepatotoxicity — this is a major clinical error. Statins are SAFE in NAFLD and NASH with mildly elevated LFTs (up to 3x ULN). The very small risk of statin-induced hepatotoxicity (<0.001%) is far outweighed by cardiovascular mortality reduction.

medicines.name: Atorvastatin
medicines.dosage: 10-80mg once daily (evening); dose based on LDL target
medicines.use_case: Dyslipidaemia in NAFLD; cardiovascular risk reduction (primary cause of death in NAFLD); all NAFLD patients with elevated LDL or cardiovascular risk factors SHOULD receive statin therapy
medicines.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor — reduces cholesterol synthesis; upregulates LDL receptors; additional anti-inflammatory and endothelial-stabilising 'pleiotropic' effects
medicines.safety_in_nafld: SAFE — statin use in NASH with elevated LFTs (<3x ULN) is recommended; monitor LFTs at baseline and 3 months; discontinue if ALT >10x ULN (drug-induced hepatotoxicity)
medicines.nash_benefit: Some observational studies show statins associated with reduced NASH progression and HCC risk; possible hepatoprotective effect beyond lipid lowering (NF-κB inhibition, antifibrotic)
side_effects: Hepatotoxicity (very rare — <0.001%; do NOT withhold due to existing elevated LFTs up to 3x ULN)
Diabetes risk (mild increase — acceptable given cardiovascular benefit)

medicines.name: Rosuvastatin
medicines.dosage: 5-40mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Dyslipidaemia; particularly useful in NAFLD with high triglycerides (modest triglyceride-lowering effect alongside strong LDL reduction)
medicines.side_effects: Similar to atorvastatin; proteinuria reported (benign — monitor)

categories.purpose: Several antidiabetic medications have beneficial effects on hepatic steatosis and NASH beyond glucose control — particularly relevant in the 70% of NAFLD patients with concurrent T2DM or prediabetes.

medicines.name: Metformin
medicines.dosage: 500mg twice daily increasing to 500-1000mg twice daily; max 2000-2500mg/day
medicines.use_case: Type 2 diabetes with NAFLD; prediabetes; insulin resistance; cardiovascular risk reduction; NOT recommended as specific NASH treatment (multiple RCTs showed no improvement in liver histology) but essential for metabolic comorbidity management
medicines.mechanism: AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) activation — reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis; mild reduction in de novo lipogenesis; weight neutral to modest weight loss
medicines.nash_histology: Multiple RCTs: metformin does NOT improve NASH histology (steatosis, inflammation, fibrosis) vs placebo — NOT recommended as specific NASH pharmacotherapy by AASLD/EASL
medicines.why_prescribe: Essential for T2DM control; reduces cardiovascular mortality; may reduce HCC risk in NAFLD patients with diabetes (observational data); first-line for T2DM with NAFLD
side_effects: GI: nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps (most common — take with food; slow-release MR formulation reduces GI side effects)
Lactic acidosis (very rare — avoid in eGFR <30; hold before contrast CT/IV contrast procedures)

medicines.name: Empagliflozin / Dapagliflozin / Canagliflozin (SGLT2 Inhibitors)
medicines.dosage: Empagliflozin: 10-25mg once daily; Dapagliflozin: 10mg once daily; Canagliflozin: 100-300mg once daily
medicines.use_case: T2DM with NAFLD — dual benefit: glucose control + NAFLD improvement; cardiovascular and renal protection in T2DM with CVD/CKD; emerging evidence for NASH histological improvement
medicines.mechanism: SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2) inhibition in proximal renal tubule — promotes urinary glucose excretion; caloric loss (~70g glucose/day); weight loss 2-3kg; reduces blood pressure; reduces hepatic de novo lipogenesis; anti-inflammatory; reduces liver fat
medicines.nash_evidence: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce hepatic steatosis (MRI-PDFF reduction 3-5%), reduce ALT and AST, reduce liver stiffness; E-LIFT trial (empagliflozin vs placebo): significant reduction in liver fat and ALT; Phase 3 NASH trials ongoing
medicines.cardiovascular_benefit: EMPA-REG OUTCOME: empagliflozin reduces cardiovascular death 38% and heart failure hospitalisation 35% in T2DM with CVD — essential in NAFLD with cardiovascular risk
medicines.renal_benefit: Proven renoprotective — reduce CKD progression in T2DM; important as NAFLD is associated with CKD
side_effects: DKA (rare but serious — hold if unwell, fasting, or major surgery)
medicines.note: SGLT2 inhibitors are increasingly considered as preferred antidiabetic agents in T2DM with NAFLD due to dual metabolic and hepatic benefits

categories.purpose: Management of alcoholic liver disease — from alcoholic fatty liver to severe alcoholic hepatitis. ALCOHOL ABSTINENCE is the single most important intervention across all stages.

medicines.name: Prednisolone (Corticosteroids — Severe Alcoholic Hepatitis)
medicines.dosage: Prednisolone 40mg orally once daily for 28 days; then taper over 2-4 weeks; assess response with Lille score at day 7
medicines.use_case: SEVERE ALCOHOLIC HEPATITIS (Maddrey's Discriminant Function ≥32 OR MELD ≥21); reduces short-term mortality; STOP if Lille score >0.45 at day 7 (non-responder)
medicines.mechanism: Anti-inflammatory — reduces hepatic neutrophilic infiltration and cytokine production (TNF-α, IL-1β); reduces hepatocyte apoptosis
medicines.lille_score_interpretation: Calculated at day 7: Lille <0.16 = complete responder (mortality <15% at 6 months); 0.16-0.45 = partial responder; >0.45 = non-responder (stop steroids — high mortality; consider liver transplant evaluation)
side_effects: Increased infection risk (monitor closely; avoid if active infection)
contraindications: Active infection (sepsis, SBP, pneumonia — treat infection first then reassess)

medicines.name: Pentoxifylline
medicines.dosage: 400mg three times daily for 28 days
medicines.use_case: Severe alcoholic hepatitis when corticosteroids are CONTRAINDICATED (infection, GI bleeding, pancreatitis, uncontrolled diabetes); anti-TNF-alpha mechanism; modest mortality benefit
medicines.mechanism: Phosphodiesterase inhibitor + TNF-alpha inhibitor — reduces hepatic inflammation; reduces hepatorenal syndrome risk
medicines.note: STOPAH trial: pentoxifylline did NOT significantly improve 28-day or 90-day mortality vs placebo; prednisolone showed modest benefit; debate continues on pentoxifylline's role

medicines.name: N-Acetylcysteine (NAC)
medicines.dosage: IV: various protocols; Oral: 600mg twice to three times daily
medicines.use_case: Adjunct to prednisolone in severe alcoholic hepatitis (improves short-term mortality when combined with prednisolone — data from Nguyen et al. trial); hepatoprotective; acetaminophen overdose (primary use)
medicines.mechanism: Precursor to glutathione — replenishes hepatic antioxidant capacity; reduces oxidative stress and hepatocyte death

medicines.name: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) + Multivitamins
medicines.dosage: Thiamine 100-500mg IV/IM before glucose administration; then 100mg orally three times daily; thiamine MUST be given BEFORE IV glucose in alcoholics
medicines.use_case: MANDATORY in all patients with ALD and alcohol use disorder — prevents and treats Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency causes irreversible brain damage — confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia)
medicines.mechanism: Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase — essential for carbohydrate metabolism and neurological function
medicines.critical_warning: NEVER give IV glucose/dextrose to an alcoholic patient without first giving IV thiamine — glucose consumption depletes already-low thiamine → precipitates acute Wernicke's encephalopathy

medicines.name: Naltrexone (Alcohol Use Disorder — Relapse Prevention)
medicines.dosage: Oral: 50mg once daily; Vivitrol: 380mg IM once monthly
medicines.use_case: Alcohol use disorder — reduces craving and relapse rate; essential component of ALD management alongside hepatology care; approved and evidence-based for alcohol dependence
medicines.mechanism: Opioid receptor antagonist — blocks opioid-mediated reward of alcohol; reduces alcohol craving and pleasurable effect
side_effects: Liver enzyme elevation (avoid if ALT >5x ULN; ALD — use with caution; monthly IM avoids daily oral peak)

medicines.name: Acamprosate
medicines.dosage: 333mg (2 tablets) three times daily; continue 1 year
medicines.use_case: Alcohol use disorder — reduces post-detoxification craving; alternative to naltrexone; safe in liver disease (renal excretion, not hepatically metabolised)
medicines.mechanism: NMDA and GABA receptor modulation — reduces neurological hyperexcitability of alcohol withdrawal and craving
medicines.advantage: Safe in liver disease (not hepatically metabolised) — preferred over naltrexone in decompensated cirrhosis

categories.purpose: Treatment of portal hypertension complications in NASH-related cirrhosis and advanced alcoholic cirrhosis.

medicines.name: Propranolol / Carvedilol (Non-selective Beta-blockers — Varices)
medicines.dosage: Propranolol: 20-40mg twice daily; titrate to resting HR 55-60 bpm; max 160mg/day. Carvedilol: 6.25-12.5mg once daily (more potent portal pressure reduction)
medicines.use_case: Primary prophylaxis against first variceal haemorrhage in patients with medium-large oesophageal varices; reduces portal pressure; reduces risk of first bleed by 50%
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective beta-blockade reduces cardiac output (beta-1) and causes splanchnic vasoconstriction (beta-2) — reduces portal pressure and variceal wall tension
side_effects: Hypotension (especially with carvedilol — higher alpha blockade)
medicines.monitoring: Target resting heart rate 55-60 bpm; BP monitoring

medicines.name: Spironolactone + Furosemide (Ascites Management)
medicines.dosage: Spironolactone 100-400mg + Furosemide 40-160mg (standard ratio 100:40 — reduces hypokalaemia risk); start: spironolactone 100mg + furosemide 40mg; titrate every 4-7 days based on response
medicines.use_case: Ascites management in cirrhosis — first-line diuretic combination; spironolactone blocks aldosterone (which promotes Na retention in cirrhosis via RAAS activation); furosemide provides additional natriuresis
medicines.monitoring: Weight daily (target 0.5-1kg/day weight loss); electrolytes every 4-7 days; creatinine and urea

medicines.name: Rifaximin + Lactulose (Hepatic Encephalopathy)
medicines.dosage: Rifaximin: 550mg twice daily; Lactulose: 15-30mL 2-3 times daily (target 2-3 soft stools per day)
medicines.use_case: Prevention and treatment of hepatic encephalopathy — ammonia-reducing strategies; lactulose promotes ammonia excretion via acidification of colonic contents; rifaximin reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria
medicines.mechanism: Lactulose: non-absorbable disaccharide — acidifies colon (pH<5.5) trapping ammonia as ammonium (NH4+) and promotes its excretion; cathartic. Rifaximin: non-absorbable oral antibiotic — reduces gut ammonia-producing bacteria
side_effects: Lactulose: bloating, flatulence, diarrhoea (excess dose), hyponatraemia (excess)
Rifaximin: generally very well tolerated; rare GI upset; minimal systemic absorption

medicines.name: Terlipressin (Hepatorenal Syndrome)
medicines.dosage: 1-2mg IV every 4-6 hours; continue until creatinine improves or maximum 14 days
medicines.use_case: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) type 1 (acute) and type 2 — splanchnic vasoconstrictor; reduces renal vasoconstriction by increasing systemic mean arterial pressure; FDA approved 2022 for HRS-AKI
side_effects: Cardiovascular ischaemia (contraindicated with ischaemic heart disease)

categories.purpose: Agents with hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory, or antifibrotic properties used as adjuncts in NAFLD management. Evidence is generally weaker than for lifestyle modification or the pharmacotherapies above.

medicines.name: Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA / UDCA)
medicines.dosage: 10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses (for PBC/PSC); 500-1000mg/day for NAFLD adjunct
medicines.use_case: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC — first-line treatment); Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC); NAFLD — limited evidence; gallstone dissolution; some centres use as adjunct in NAFLD for cholestatic symptoms
medicines.mechanism: Hydrophilic bile acid — replaces hydrophobic toxic bile acids; cytoprotective; immunomodulatory; anti-apoptotic
medicines.nash_evidence: Multiple RCTs: UDCA at standard doses does NOT improve NASH histology (vs placebo); higher doses (28-35 mg/kg/day) showed some benefit in small trials — not standard therapy

medicines.name: Silymarin (Milk Thistle — Silybum marianum)
medicines.dosage: 140-420mg three times daily (silymarin content — look for standardised extract containing 70-80% silymarin)
medicines.use_case: Hepatoprotective adjunct in NAFLD and ALD; widely used in India and globally; some evidence for antifibrotic and anti-inflammatory effects; NOT a replacement for lifestyle modification or pharmacotherapy
medicines.mechanism: Mixture of flavonolignans (silybin, silychristin, silydianin) — antioxidant; anti-inflammatory (reduces NF-κB, TNF-α); antifibrotic (reduces HSC activation); promotes hepatocyte protein synthesis
medicines.evidence: Multiple small RCTs showing ALT and AST improvement; meta-analyses suggest modest benefit on liver enzymes in NAFLD; one RCT (FLORA trial) showed fibrosis improvement; not included in major guidelines but widely used clinically
medicines.note: Not recommended as monotherapy for NASH/MASH by major guidelines; can be used as adjunct alongside lifestyle modification

medicines.name: Omega-3 Fatty Acids (Fish Oil — EPA/DHA)
medicines.dosage: 1-4g EPA+DHA daily with meals
medicines.use_case: Hypertriglyceridaemia in NAFLD (omega-3 approved for severe hypertriglyceridaemia); hepatic steatosis reduction (adjunct); anti-inflammatory; cardiovascular risk reduction
medicines.mechanism: EPA and DHA — reduces hepatic de novo lipogenesis; activates PPAR-alpha (promotes fatty acid oxidation); reduces VLDL production; anti-inflammatory (resolvin and protectin synthesis); reduces triglycerides 30-50% at 4g/day
medicines.nash_evidence: Multiple RCTs: omega-3 reduces liver fat (MRI-PDFF), reduces triglycerides, reduces ALT; conflicting data on histological NASH improvement; AASLD: not recommended as primary NASH pharmacotherapy but acceptable for coexisting hypertriglyceridaemia
side_effects: Fishy aftertaste and burping (take with food; refrigerate; use enteric-coated)
Slight antiplatelet effect — caution with warfarin at high doses

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet is the most powerful intervention for fatty liver disease. The Mediterranean diet is the most evidence-based dietary pattern for NAFLD/MASLD — associated with lower NAFLD prevalence, reduced hepatic steatosis, and improved metabolic parameters in multiple studies. The core principles are: reduce refined carbohydrates and added sugars (particularly fructose), eliminate or drastically reduce alcohol, reduce saturated fats, increase fibre and antioxidants, achieve caloric deficit for weight loss, and avoid ultra-processed foods. Coffee consumption is uniquely hepatoprotective — one of the most consistent findings in hepatology.

caloric_targets.weight_loss: 500-1000 kcal daily deficit for 0.5-1 kg/week weight loss; 7-10% body weight reduction target for NASH resolution (takes 12-24 months with sustained effort)
caloric_targets.maintenance: Euocaloric Mediterranean diet once target weight achieved
caloric_targets.very_low_calorie: Very Low Calorie Diets (VLCD — 800 kcal/day) or low-calorie diets (LCD — 1200-1500 kcal/day) under medical supervision can achieve rapid significant weight loss — effective for NASH resolution but difficult to sustain

recommended_foods.evidence: VERY STRONG — one of the most robust findings in hepatology. Regular coffee consumption (≥2-3 cups/day) is independently and consistently associated with: 40-50% lower risk of liver fibrosis progression; 40% lower risk of hepatocellular carcinoma; lower ALT and AST; reduced liver stiffness on FibroScan; protection against progression from NAFLD to NASH. Effect appears to be from caffeine AND non-caffeine components (chlorogenic acids, diterpenes, antioxidants) — protective even with decaffeinated coffee.

items.food: Coffee (filtered, espresso, or instant — all types with evidence)
items.benefit: Hepatoprotective through multiple mechanisms: reduces liver fibrosis (inhibits HSC activation); antioxidant (reduces ROS); reduces hepatic de novo lipogenesis; anti-inflammatory (reduces TNF-α and IL-6); reduces HCC risk (apoptosis of hepatocytes with malignant potential)
items.frequency: 2-3 cups daily (caffeinated or decaffeinated) — recommend as part of NAFLD management
items.note: Drink without sugar and avoid with high-fat creamers or full-fat milk (negate metabolic benefits)

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — MEDINA trial and multiple observational studies show Mediterranean diet reduces hepatic steatosis, reduces NASH activity, and improves metabolic markers in NAFLD

items.benefit: Rich in oleocanthal (anti-inflammatory — COX inhibitor similar to ibuprofen) and oleic acid (monounsaturated fat); reduces hepatic inflammation; reduces de novo lipogenesis; improves insulin sensitivity; reduces LDL oxidation. EVOO is the primary fat in Mediterranean diet — replace butter and saturated fats.
items.frequency: 2-3 tablespoons daily for cooking or salad dressing (moderate — high calorie density)
items.note: Cold-pressed, unfiltered EVOO has highest polyphenol content; avoid heating at high temperatures (degrades polyphenols)

items.food: Oily fish: Salmon, Mackerel, Sardines, Tuna, Trout
items.benefit: High EPA and DHA omega-3 fatty acids — reduce hepatic triglyceride synthesis; reduce VLDL production; anti-inflammatory (reduce TNF-α, IL-6); improve insulin sensitivity; reduce cardiovascular risk (leading cause of death in NAFLD)

items.food: Vegetables (all varieties — especially cruciferous and dark leafy)
items.benefit: Low-calorie; high-fibre; rich in antioxidants and polyphenols; anti-inflammatory; support gut microbiome diversity; reduce hepatic inflammation. Cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts) contain sulforaphane — specific antifibrotic properties in animal models. Dark leafy greens provide Vitamin K, folate, magnesium.
items.frequency: Minimum 5-7 servings daily; aim to fill half the plate with vegetables
specific: Beetroot (betaine — reduces hepatic steatosis; methyl donor)
Spinach, kale, Swiss chard (antioxidants, Vitamin K)

items.food: Legumes: Lentils, Chickpeas, Kidney beans, Black beans, Dal
items.benefit: High plant protein; low glycaemic index (reduces insulin spikes); high soluble fibre (promotes beneficial gut bacteria; reduces LPS translocation — key NASH driver); low in saturated fat; reduces postprandial triglyceridaemia
items.frequency: Daily — dal, chana, rajma — excellent for Indian dietary context

items.food: Whole grains: Brown rice, Whole wheat, Oats, Barley, Quinoa
items.benefit: Complex carbohydrates with low glycaemic index — reduce insulin spikes and de novo lipogenesis; high fibre (especially beta-glucan in oats — reduces cholesterol and improves insulin sensitivity); B vitamins for hepatic metabolism
items.frequency: 3-6 servings daily; replace all refined carbohydrates with whole grain equivalents

items.benefit: Walnuts highest in plant omega-3 (ALA) and polyphenols — associated with lower NAFLD risk and reduced hepatic steatosis in observational studies. Almonds: Vitamin E, monounsaturated fats. All nuts: satiating, fibre, protein — support caloric control.
items.frequency: Daily small handful (30g) — high calorie density; portion control essential
items.clinical_study: Walnuts study (San Diego) — 1.5 oz walnuts daily × 6 months: significant liver fat reduction vs control diet

items.benefit: Antioxidants, polyphenols, fibre; blueberries and cherries specifically associated with antifibrotic effects (anthocyanins inhibit HSC activation); pomegranate (punicalagins reduce hepatic inflammation)
items.frequency: 2-3 servings daily — whole fruit preferred over juice (juice = concentrated fructose without fibre)
items.caution: Limit high-sugar fruits (grapes, mango, banana, ripe dates) and fruit juices; fructose directly drives hepatic de novo lipogenesis

items.benefit: Lean protein without saturated fat excess; supports caloric deficit; provides amino acids for hepatic protein synthesis
items.frequency: 3-4 servings per week (baked, grilled — not fried)

items.benefit: High-quality complete protein; sulphur amino acids (cysteine, methionine) support glutathione synthesis (hepatic antioxidant); low in saturated fat (egg white); choline in yolk important for hepatic fat export (VLDL — choline deficiency causes fatty liver paradoxically)
items.frequency: 3-5 whole eggs per week; unlimited egg whites; choline from eggs may actually be beneficial for NAFLD

items.benefit: Plant protein; isoflavones may reduce hepatic steatosis; fibre; low saturated fat; alternative to red meat
items.frequency: 3-4 times per week as meat alternative

items.benefit: Curcumin: anti-inflammatory (reduces NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-6); antifibrotic (inhibits TGF-beta1, reduces HSC activation); reduces hepatic de novo lipogenesis; antioxidant; Phase 2 trials in NASH show significant ALT and AST reduction; improves insulin sensitivity
items.frequency: 1 tsp turmeric daily in cooking or warm milk (add piperine/black pepper to increase bioavailability 2000%)
items.evidence: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses support curcumin for NAFLD (reduces ALT, AST, liver fat, inflammatory markers)

items.benefit: EGCG polyphenol: antioxidant; reduces hepatic fat (de novo lipogenesis suppression); anti-inflammatory; improves insulin sensitivity; reduces LDL oxidation; associated with lower NAFLD risk in cohort studies
items.frequency: 2-3 cups daily (without sugar); green tea extract supplements also used

items.benefit: Allicin and organosulphur compounds: antioxidant; reduces hepatic inflammation; inhibits HSC activation (antifibrotic potential); reduces triglycerides and LDL cholesterol; anti-inflammatory
items.frequency: 1-2 raw cloves daily or in cooking; aged garlic extract supplements

items.food: Grapefruit (and grapefruit juice — caution with medications)
