items.benefit: Naringenin (flavonoid) — reduces hepatic de novo lipogenesis; reduces VLDL synthesis; improves insulin sensitivity; reduces fasting glucose. Animal models: significant liver fat reduction.
items.caution: Grapefruit STRONGLY inhibits CYP3A4 — interacts with many medications (statins, immunosuppressants, some antidiabetic drugs — check interactions); avoid if on multiple medications
items.frequency: Moderate consumption if medication-free or interactions checked

items.benefit: Betaine (trimethylglycine) — a methyl donor; reduces hepatic lipid accumulation; improves methionine metabolism; reduces oxidative stress; betaine is specifically used as a research agent in NASH studies; nitrates improve liver blood flow
Cynarin and luteolin: hepatoprotective; stimulates bile secretion; reduces cholesterol and triglycerides; improves liver function in small trials; antioxidant
items.frequency: 2-3 times per week; artichoke leaf extract supplement also used

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — gut dysbiosis is a key NAFLD pathogenesis mechanism; restoring microbiome diversity reduces LPS translocation and hepatic inflammation

items.food: Prebiotic fibre: Garlic, Onion, Leek, Asparagus, Jerusalem artichoke, Chicory, Oats, Barley
items.benefit: Feeds beneficial gut bacteria (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium); increases short-chain fatty acid (SCFA — butyrate) production which seals intestinal tight junctions and reduces LPS translocation to portal circulation; reduces hepatic inflammation

items.food: Probiotic foods: Plain yogurt (with live cultures), Kefir, Kimchi, Miso, Idli/Dosa
items.benefit: Restores gut microbiome diversity; reduces intestinal permeability; reduces systemic LPS levels; reduces hepatic TNF-α and IL-6 activation; clinical trial evidence for VSL#3 probiotic improving NASH (reduced steatosis, ALT, fibrosis markers)
items.frequency: Daily probiotic yogurt; probiotic supplement (VSL#3, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG) alongside diet

foods_to_avoid.food: Added sugars — especially Fructose (MOST CRITICAL avoidance)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Fructose is THE primary dietary driver of NAFLD. Unlike glucose, fructose is exclusively metabolised by the liver — overwhelming hepatic fructose-1-phosphate pathways drives de novo lipogenesis, triglyceride synthesis, uric acid production (activates NLRP3 inflammasome), and hepatic insulin resistance. Dietary fructose from sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) is particularly harmful (liquid fructose absorbed very rapidly).
foods_to_avoid.mechanism: Fructokinase catalyses fructose phosphorylation in liver → depletes ATP (fructose-1-phosphate) → activates de novo lipogenesis via ChREBP and SREBP-1c → triglyceride synthesis; also activates NLRP3 inflammasome via uric acid production → hepatic inflammation
examples: Sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs): cola, Pepsi, Fanta, fruit sodas — the most harmful NAFLD dietary item
Fruit juice (including 100% fruit juice — high fructose without fibre)
Sweet lassi, packaged flavoured milk, flavoured yoghurt
Honey and agave syrup (very high fructose)
High-fructose corn syrup (HFCS) in packaged foods — read labels
foods_to_avoid.evidence: NHANES data: each additional SSB per day increases NAFLD odds by 56%; SSB consumption of ≥1/day associated with 2x greater hepatic steatosis

foods_to_avoid.reason: Alcohol is directly hepatotoxic at every stage of liver disease. Even 'moderate' alcohol consumption worsens NAFLD progression. In NAFLD: alcohol synergistically worsens steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis (alcohol and metabolic steatosis share inflammatory pathways — additive damage). In ALD: any alcohol perpetuates and accelerates disease. In cirrhosis: any alcohol dramatically increases decompensation risk and mortality.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: COMPLETE ABSTINENCE for all patients with ALD. <7 units/week for NAFLD patients (ideally abstain — the new MASLD definition allows moderate alcohol consumption, but safest recommendation is to avoid)
foods_to_avoid.alcohol_synergy: Alcohol + obesity: synergistic liver damage — each 10-unit increase in weekly alcohol in BMI>30 individuals increases cirrhosis risk far more than either alone

foods_to_avoid.reason: Refined carbohydrates (white rice, white bread, pasta, maida) cause rapid glucose spikes → hyperinsulinaemia → hepatic de novo lipogenesis via SREBP-1c activation. Ultra-processed foods (UPF) contain harmful additives, emulsifiers, and preservatives that disrupt gut microbiome, promote intestinal permeability, and increase hepatic inflammation.
examples: White bread, white rice (substitute whole grain), plain flour (maida)
Ready meals and frozen processed food

foods_to_avoid.reason: Saturated fatty acids (SFAs — palmitate especially) are lipotoxic — cause direct hepatocyte injury, ER stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and activate TLR4 on Kupffer cells promoting inflammation. Trans fats disrupt membrane fluidity, impair insulin signalling, and cause hepatic inflammation.
examples: Full-fat dairy (cream, butter, full-fat cheese, ghee in excess)
Coconut oil (very high in saturated fat — 92% — despite popular claims)
Hydrogenated vegetable oils (trans fats — in many commercial bakery products)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Haem iron in red meat promotes hepatic oxidative stress and ferroptosis; processed meats contain nitrates and advanced glycation end products (AGEs) which trigger hepatic inflammation; associated with NAFLD and HCC risk in epidemiological studies
examples: Processed meats: salami, sausages, hot dogs, bacon, corned beef
Excessive red meat: beef, lamb, pork (>100g/day)
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Limit red meat to <2 servings per week; avoid all processed meats

foods_to_avoid.reason: High GI foods cause rapid glucose spikes, stimulate insulin release, activate SREBP-1c and ChREBP transcription factors, and directly promote hepatic de novo lipogenesis. In NAFLD patients with insulin resistance, high-GI foods have amplified metabolic harm.
foods_to_avoid.low_GI_alternatives: Brown rice, whole wheat bread, oats, sweet potato, legumes, most vegetables

foods_to_avoid.food: Excessive salt and processed salty snacks
foods_to_avoid.reason: High sodium promotes hypertension (major MASLD comorbidity); excessive salt intake associated with metabolic syndrome; salt-preserved foods contain nitrites; salty ultra-processed snacks are high in refined carbohydrates and saturated fat
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: <2.3g sodium (5.75g salt) per day; ideally <1.5g sodium for hypertensive NAFLD patients

sample_meal_plan.note: This Mediterranean-NAFLD meal plan targets 7-10% body weight loss, reduces hepatic steatosis, and improves metabolic parameters. It is calorie-controlled (~1600-1800 kcal/day). Coffee is included for hepatoprotection. Zero alcohol, zero added sugars, zero ultra-processed foods.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: 2 glasses of water + 1 tablespoon apple cider vinegar in warm water (optional — some evidence for insulin sensitising effect) + soaked almonds (7-8) or walnuts (5-6)
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal with chia seeds, walnuts, and blueberries (no added sugar — use cinnamon) OR 2-egg vegetable omelette with whole wheat toast (1 slice) + 1 cup filter coffee (no sugar; skimmed milk)
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: Green tea (2nd cup) OR herbal tea + 1 apple or pear (whole fruit — not juice) + small handful roasted pumpkin seeds
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Brown rice (small portion — 1/2 cup cooked) + moong/masoor dal + sabzi (spinach, broccoli, or mixed vegetables with minimal oil — use olive oil or mustard oil) + 1 cup plain curd + salad (cucumber, tomato, carrot, beetroot) with olive oil and lemon dressing
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: 3rd coffee or green tea (no sugar) + roasted chickpeas or edamame OR 1-2 walnuts + 1 fruit
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Grilled fish (salmon or mackerel) or tofu/paneer (small portion) + 2 chapati (whole wheat — no ghee) + sabzi (mixed vegetables) + small bowl rajma or chana + cucumber raita (low-fat curd)
sample_meal_plan.post_dinner: Warm turmeric milk (skimmed milk + 1/2 tsp turmeric + pinch black pepper) OR chamomile tea — NO eating after dinner; minimum 12-14 hours overnight fast (time-restricted eating benefits for NAFLD)
sample_meal_plan.hydration: 2.5-3 litres water daily throughout; 2-3 cups coffee daily; herbal teas; avoid fruit juices, sodas, and alcohol completely

special_dietary_notes: WEIGHT LOSS is the most important dietary outcome — even 5% weight loss reduces liver fat significantly; 7-10% achieves NASH resolution in many patients; sustained weight loss is more important than the type of diet
FRUCTOSE elimination from sugar-sweetened beverages is the single highest-impact dietary change — immediately reduces hepatic lipogenesis
COFFEE (2-3 cups/day) is the most evidence-based hepatoprotective dietary recommendation — prescribe coffee as part of NAFLD management

TIME-RESTRICTED EATING (16:8 intermittent fasting — eating within an 8-hour window) reduces hepatic steatosis independently of caloric restriction; metabolic benefits include improved insulin sensitivity and reduced de novo lipogenesis; safe and practical approach for NAFLD

KETOGENIC DIET (very low carbohydrate, high fat): rapidly reduces liver fat and improves insulin sensitivity short-term; concerns about sustainability, LDL elevation, and long-term effects; not recommended as first-line but may suit some patients short-term under supervision

CHOLINE supplementation: choline is essential for hepatic VLDL assembly and fat export from liver; deficiency promotes fatty liver; eggs, legumes, and cruciferous vegetables are good dietary sources; choline supplement 500-1000mg/day in patients with dietary deficiency

GUT MICROBIOME dietary support: prebiotic fibre (artichoke, leek, garlic, oats, chicory) and probiotic foods (yogurt, kefir) are increasingly important therapeutic targets in NAFLD management through the gut-liver axis

weight_loss.evidence: MOST EFFECTIVE INTERVENTION for NAFLD. Evidence from multiple trials: 5% weight loss reduces hepatic steatosis; 7% resolves NASH histologically in ~50%; 10% improves fibrosis; >10% achieves NASH resolution with fibrosis improvement in most patients. Bariatric surgery achieves the greatest sustained weight loss — most powerful intervention for severe NAFLD/NASH.

targets.maintenance: Sustained weight loss; weight regain reverses all histological improvements

weight_loss_approaches: Calorie-restricted Mediterranean diet (500-1000 kcal/day deficit) — most evidence-based dietary approach
Low-carbohydrate diet — comparable weight loss to low-fat; particularly effective for insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia
Structured commercial weight loss programmes under dietitian supervision
GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) — pharmacotherapy for obesity with concurrent MASH benefit
Bariatric surgery — most effective for BMI >35 with NAFLD/NASH; sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass both improve NASH histologically

physical_exercise.evidence: Strong — exercise reduces hepatic fat content independently of weight loss (through mechanisms including increased fatty acid oxidation, reduced de novo lipogenesis, and improved insulin sensitivity). Both aerobic and resistance exercise are beneficial.

aerobic_exercise.type: Moderate-intensity: brisk walking, cycling, swimming, jogging, dancing
aerobic_exercise.target: 150-200 minutes of moderate-intensity per week (30 min × 5 days minimum); or 75-100 min vigorous-intensity
aerobic_exercise.intensity: Moderate: 50-70% maximum heart rate; perceived exertion 5-6/10 (can talk but slightly breathless)
aerobic_exercise.hepatic_fat: Aerobic exercise alone reduces liver fat 4-10% (MRI-PDFF) even without significant weight loss — direct hepatic metabolic effect

resistance_training.type: Weight training, resistance bands, body weight exercises
resistance_training.frequency: 2-3 sessions per week; 8-10 exercises; 2-3 sets of 8-12 repetitions
resistance_training.benefit: Increases skeletal muscle mass — the primary peripheral glucose disposal organ; improves insulin sensitivity; reduces liver fat independently
resistance_training.hepatic_fat: Resistance exercise reduces liver fat 3-6% — comparable to aerobic exercise; combination of both superior to either alone

recommended_type.combined_approach: Aerobic + resistance training combined — most effective for liver fat reduction, metabolic improvement, and cardiovascular risk reduction

practical_indian_context: Brisk walking (30-45 min daily) — most accessible; start with 15 min and increase
Yoga — reduces insulin resistance; stress reduction beneficial for liver; specific hepatoprotective yoga asanas
Cycling (stationary or outdoor) — non-impact; good for obese patients with joint issues
Swimming — excellent for obese patients (reduced joint load); full body workout

alcohol_management.ALD_patients: COMPLETE ABSTINENCE is mandatory — no safe level of alcohol in ALD, alcoholic hepatitis, or ALD-cirrhosis. Abstinence should be supported with: motivational interviewing; addiction specialist referral; pharmacotherapy (naltrexone, acamprosate, baclofen — for alcohol use disorder); psychosocial support; AA (Alcoholics Anonymous) or SMART Recovery programmes.
alcohol_management.NAFLD_patients: Strong recommendation to minimise or eliminate alcohol. While the new MASLD definition allows moderate alcohol (<14 units/week men; <7 units/week women), the safest recommendation for all NAFLD patients is to minimise alcohol — even moderate amounts worsen fibrosis progression in NAFLD.
alcohol_management.withdrawal_management: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (seizures, delirium tremens) must be medically supervised — never abruptly withdraw from heavy alcohol use without medical support. Benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide reducing regimen — CIWA-Ar guided) standard of care for alcohol detoxification.

sleep_and_metabolic_management: OSA management: CPAP therapy for obstructive sleep apnoea (present in 30-50% of NAFLD patients) — may modestly improve liver function and reduces metabolic syndrome severity
Sleep hygiene: 7-8 hours quality sleep; sleep deprivation increases insulin resistance and promotes weight gain
Diabetes management: optimal glycaemic control (HbA1c <53 mmol/mol / 7%); prefer SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 agonists in T2DM with NAFLD (dual metabolic and hepatic benefit)

Dyslipidaemia management: statin therapy for elevated LDL (safe in NAFLD; reduces cardiovascular mortality — primary cause of death); fibrates (fenofibrate) for hypertriglyceridaemia as adjunct to omega-3
Hypertension management: ACE inhibitors or ARBs may have modest antifibrotic benefit in NAFLD with hypertension (angiotensin II promotes HSC activation); CCBs as alternative
Thyroid optimisation: normalise TSH if hypothyroid — treats contributing cause of NAFLD
PCOS management: metformin reduces insulin resistance; GLP-1 agonists for weight and metabolic syndrome
stress_and_psychological_support: Psychological stress promotes cortisol release — cortisol increases hepatic de novo lipogenesis and promotes visceral fat accumulation
Depression and anxiety are prevalent in NAFLD — bidirectional relationship (fatigue and poor body image from NAFLD; depression worsening metabolic self-care)
CBT for weight management and metabolic behaviour change
Mindfulness and stress reduction improve metabolic outcomes
Address NASH-related stigma and body image; avoid stigmatising language ('fatty liver' can cause shame — prefer 'metabolic liver disease')
Support groups for NAFLD patients — NASH Patient Advocacy Foundation; NASH Education Program

fatty_liver_monitoring_plan.note: Fatty liver disease monitoring tracks disease progression, treatment response, and complication development. The frequency and investigations depend on fibrosis stage. Non-invasive tests (FIB-4, FibroScan) are preferred for monitoring — repeat liver biopsy only when non-invasive tests are discordant or when clinical decision pivots on histological result.

green_zone.status: Low Risk — Simple Steatosis, Well-Controlled Metabolic Disease
green_zone.criteria: FIB-4 <1.3; FibroScan <7 kPa; Normal or near-normal ALT (<2x ULN); HbA1c <53 mmol/mol; BMI showing sustained downward trend; no alarm symptoms; metabolic risk factors well-controlled
green_zone.action: Lifestyle modification continued; metabolic comorbidity treatment; annual LFTs and metabolic panel (HbA1c, lipids, glucose); FIB-4 recalculation annually; FibroScan every 2-3 years; liver ultrasound every 2-3 years; annual cardiovascular risk review. Continue coffee, Mediterranean diet, and exercise.

yellow_zone.status: Intermediate Risk — Indeterminate Fibrosis or Poorly Controlled Metabolic Disease
yellow_zone.criteria: FIB-4 1.3-2.67 (indeterminate); FibroScan 7-13 kPa; ALT persistently 2-5x ULN; weight gain or inadequate weight loss response; HbA1c >8% (uncontrolled diabetes); triglycerides >500 mg/dL; fatigue and RUQ discomfort
yellow_zone.action: Hepatology referral within 4-8 weeks. FibroScan if not yet performed. Consider liver biopsy if non-invasive tests discordant. Intensify lifestyle intervention (dietitian referral, structured exercise programme). Pharmacotherapy review — add pioglitazone (if T2DM), Vitamin E (if non-diabetic), or GLP-1 agonist (if obesity or T2DM). Manage metabolic comorbidities aggressively. 3-6 monthly LFTs.

red_zone.status: URGENT — Advanced Fibrosis, Cirrhosis, or Decompensation
red_zone.criteria: Any of: FIB-4 >2.67 or FibroScan >13 kPa (possible cirrhosis); Platelets <150,000/µL (hypersplenism); ALT or AST rapidly rising; Jaundice appearing (bilirubin rising); Ascites or oedema developing; Haematemesis or melaena; Hepatic encephalopathy (confusion); HCC suspicious lesion on ultrasound (AFP rising); Acute severe alcoholic hepatitis (jaundice + fever + tender hepatomegaly after heavy drinking)
red_zone.action: URGENT hepatology referral (within 1-2 weeks for advanced fibrosis; SAME DAY for decompensation or GI bleeding). For variceal bleeding — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES. For AH: hospital admission; Maddrey score; prednisolone if MDF ≥32. For suspected HCC: urgent multiphasic CT or MRI within 2 weeks. Six-monthly HCC surveillance if not already initiated. Transplant evaluation if MELD ≥15.

complications.description: The most common serious complication of NASH — progressive fibrosis accumulating over 10-20 years to complete architectural disruption of the liver. NASH-cirrhosis is the 3rd leading indication for liver transplant in the USA and is rising. Once cirrhosis develops, patients have significantly increased morbidity and mortality from portal hypertension complications and HCC.
complications.prevalence: ~20% of NASH patients develop cirrhosis over 20 years; rate accelerated by obesity, T2DM, and genetic variants
complications.management: Treat underlying metabolic disease; portal hypertension management; HCC surveillance; transplant evaluation

complications.description: Liver cancer arising from hepatocytes — the most feared complication of NASH-cirrhosis. HCC risk increases dramatically with cirrhosis (1-4%/year in cirrhosis). Uniquely, NASH can cause HCC even in non-cirrhotic patients (in contrast to HBV/HCV-related HCC which almost always requires cirrhosis). The rising incidence of NAFLD is driving an epidemic of NASH-related HCC globally.
complications.annual_risk: Cirrhotic NAFLD: 1-4% per year; Non-cirrhotic NASH: much lower (~0.04-0.3%/year); highest with PNPLA3 I148M variant
complications.prevention: Six-monthly ultrasound ± AFP in all NAFLD-cirrhosis patients; treat underlying metabolic disease; statins and aspirin (emerging evidence for chemoprevention); coffee consumption

complications.complication: Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) — Primary Cause of Mortality in Early NAFLD
complications.description: NAFLD is not just a liver disease — it is strongly associated with and promotes cardiovascular disease. In patients without advanced fibrosis, cardiovascular mortality is the PRIMARY cause of death (more common than liver-related death). NAFLD is an independent cardiovascular risk factor — associated with endothelial dysfunction, accelerated atherosclerosis, arterial stiffness, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure.
complications.mechanisms: Dyslipidaemia (elevated ApoB, triglycerides, small dense LDL); systemic inflammation (elevated CRP, IL-6, TNF-α); insulin resistance; elevated liver-derived prothrombotic factors
complications.severity: Severe — leading cause of death in NAFLD patients without advanced fibrosis
complications.management: Aggressive cardiovascular risk factor management: statin therapy (essential — not contraindicated in NAFLD); blood pressure control; glucose optimisation; weight loss; smoking cessation; antiplatelet therapy if indicated

complications.complication: Portal Hypertension — Variceal Haemorrhage, Ascites, Encephalopathy
complications.description: Elevated portal venous pressure from hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis causes the spectrum of portal hypertension complications. Variceal haemorrhage: rupture of oesophageal or gastric varices — presents with sudden massive haematemesis; 15-20% mortality per episode. Ascites: fluid accumulation in peritoneal cavity from portal hypertension + hypoalbuminaemia — affects quality of life; risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP — life-threatening).
complications.management: Variceal haemorrhage: EMERGENCY (IV terlipressin; antibiotics; urgent endoscopy for banding); prophylaxis with propranolol; endoscopic variceal ligation. Ascites: sodium restriction; diuretics (spironolactone + furosemide); large-volume paracentesis; TIPSS for refractory ascites

complications.description: Life-threatening infection of ascitic fluid — occurs without any bowel perforation or other obvious source. Common causative bacteria: E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcal species. Presents with fever, abdominal pain, and deteriorating liver function in a cirrhotic patient with ascites. Diagnosed by diagnostic paracentesis (PMN >250 cells/µL in ascitic fluid).
complications.management: IV antibiotics (cefotaxime 2g every 8h × 5 days); IV albumin (reduces hepatorenal syndrome risk); long-term norfloxacin prophylaxis after first episode

complications.description: Neuropsychiatric syndrome from hepatic failure to detoxify ammonia and other toxins from portal circulation — portosystemic shunting and hepatocyte dysfunction. Ranges from minimal (subtle cognitive impairment — grade I) to severe (stupor, coma — grade IV). Precipitating factors: GI bleeding, infection (SBP), constipation, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, benzodiazepines.
complications.management: Treat precipitating cause; lactulose (2-4 times/day — target 2-3 soft stools); rifaximin (550mg twice daily) for recurrent encephalopathy prevention; dietary protein — adequate protein intake essential (malnutrition worsens encephalopathy paradoxically; restrict protein only in acute severe encephalopathy)

complications.description: NAFLD is independently associated with CKD — 30-50% of NAFLD patients develop CKD. Shared pathophysiological pathways: insulin resistance, systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction. NAFLD doubles CKD progression risk. ALD-cirrhosis frequently complicated by hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) — functional renal failure from severe portal hypertension.
complications.management: Treat underlying metabolic disease; SGLT2 inhibitors (renoprotective); avoid nephrotoxic drugs; monitor eGFR and urine ACR annually

complications.description: NAFLD is associated with increased risk of colorectal cancer (1.8x), breast cancer (oestrogen-excess from liver dysfunction), and pancreatic cancer. Mechanisms likely include systemic hyperinsulinaemia, inflammation, and IGF-1 signalling. Important to maintain cancer screening programmes in NAFLD patients.
complications.management: Age-appropriate cancer screening; colonoscopy (colorectal cancer); breast screening; lifestyle modification reduces cancer risk

complications.description: Advanced liver disease impairs hepatic synthesis of clotting factors (all except von Willebrand factor and factor VIII are synthesised by the liver) → prolonged PT/INR. Portal hypertension causes hypersplenism → thrombocytopenia. Paradoxically, cirrhosis is not simply a 'bleeding disorder' — it is actually a state of rebalanced haemostasis (both pro- and anticoagulant factors reduced) with risk of BOTH bleeding AND thrombosis.
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe in advanced disease
complications.management: Vitamin K (for vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency); FFP (fresh frozen plasma) and platelets before invasive procedures; avoid unnecessary blood thinners

key_points: T2DM is the single strongest predictor of NASH and advanced fibrosis in NAFLD — 70% of T2DM patients have NAFLD; 30-40% have NASH

Preferred antidiabetic drugs in T2DM with NAFLD: GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) — dual metabolic and hepatic benefit; SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) — renoprotective, cardiovascular benefit, reduces liver fat; Pioglitazone — improves NASH histology but causes weight gain

AVOID in advanced NAFLD-cirrhosis: Metformin (lactic acidosis risk in decompensated cirrhosis — hold if MELD >10); Pioglitazone (fluid retention — worsens ascites); Sulphonylureas (hypoglycaemia risk — impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis in cirrhosis)
HbA1c may be falsely LOW in cirrhosis (reduced red cell survival, haemolysis) — use fructosamine or glucose monitoring instead
Annual retinal and renal screening essential in T2DM-NAFLD
Paediatric NAFLD is a global epidemic — rising with childhood obesity; affects 3-10% of all children; 35-40% of obese children
Presentation often at metabolic screening or incidentally on ultrasound; rarely symptomatic
Children with NAFLD have unique histological features: portal-predominant inflammation (vs centrilobular in adults)
Primary cause is obesity with insulin resistance — management focuses on lifestyle intervention (family-based intervention most effective in children)

Pharmacological treatment: limited approved options in children. Vitamin E may be used (evidence from TONIC trial — no significant histological benefit); GLP-1 agonists (liraglutide approved from 12 years for obesity — SCALE Teens trial); metformin for T2DM
Avoid pioglitazone (insufficient paediatric evidence); bariatric surgery considered in severely obese adolescents ≥16 years with severe NASH
Metabolic screening: fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, ALT in all overweight children (BMI ≥85th percentile)
Pre-existing NAFLD worsens during pregnancy due to: pregnancy-related weight gain, insulin resistance of pregnancy, and increased metabolic demand
AFLP (Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy) is a distinct, life-threatening condition — not simple NAFLD — caused by LCHAD enzyme deficiency in fetus; occurs in 3rd trimester
AFLP presents with: jaundice, RUQ pain, nausea, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia — diagnosis by Swansea criteria
IMMEDIATE DELIVERY is definitive treatment for AFLP — regardless of gestational age
Pre-existing NAFLD increases risk of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and preterm birth

NAFLD medications: metformin safe; statins CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (teratogenic); pioglitazone CONTRAINDICATED; GLP-1 agonists CONTRAINDICATED; resmetirom CONTRAINDICATED — use lifestyle measures and insulin for diabetes
Vitamin E (food sources not high-dose supplements) and Mediterranean diet safe in pregnancy
Bariatric surgery is the most effective weight loss intervention for NAFLD — significant histological NASH resolution and fibrosis improvement
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB): most liver benefit — metabolic advantages beyond weight loss (gut hormone changes improve insulin sensitivity)
Sleeve gastrectomy: good liver benefit; occasionally may worsen GERD (relative contraindication to sleeve if severe GERD)
Post-bariatric NAFLD monitoring: LFTs and liver ultrasound at 6 months and 1 year post-surgery; most patients show significant improvement
Rare: accelerated NASH progression post-bariatric surgery from rapid weight loss (protein-calorie malnutrition) — nutritional support essential; avoid very rapid weight loss

Early liver transplantation (early LT) for severe alcoholic hepatitis non-responders to medical treatment: selected programmes transplanting patients with <6 months abstinence (historically required 6-month sobriety period); European data shows similar post-transplant outcomes with careful patient selection (RESILIENT study)
Female vulnerability: women develop ALD at lower alcohol doses, faster progression, and more severe disease — alcoholic cirrhosis at 40-60% lower cumulative dose than men
Nutritional support is critical in alcoholic hepatitis: enteral feeding (nasogastric tube if oral intake inadequate) — malnutrition is an independent mortality predictor in AH
Zinc deficiency is universal in ALD — zinc supplementation 220mg twice daily (zinc sulfate) improves liver function and reduces infection risk
Alcohol use disorder comorbidities: depression, anxiety, PTSD — address psychiatric comorbidities alongside hepatology care

vaccinations_recommended.reason: CRITICAL for all patients with chronic liver disease including NAFLD, ALD, and cirrhosis. Superimposed HAV infection on pre-existing liver disease causes significantly higher morbidity and mortality (acute liver failure rate higher in underlying liver disease). HAV vaccination is MANDATORY recommended for all patients with any chronic liver disease per EASL, AASLD, and NICE guidelines.
vaccinations_recommended.note: All NAFLD patients should have HAV serology checked; if non-immune — vaccinate

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 3-dose series (0, 1, 6 months); check anti-HBs titre 4-8 weeks after 3rd dose; revaccinate if <10 IU/L
vaccinations_recommended.reason: CRITICAL — co-infection of NAFLD with HBV dramatically accelerates fibrosis progression and HCC risk. All NAFLD patients should be screened for HBV immunity (anti-HBs) — if non-immune, vaccinate urgently. HBV superinfection on pre-existing cirrhosis can cause acute decompensation and liver failure.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Combined Hepatitis A + B vaccine (Twinrix) provides protection with one 3-dose course — preferred for efficiency

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients with chronic liver disease have significantly impaired hepatic immune function. Influenza causes systemic inflammation that can precipitate acute decompensation in cirrhosis. Influenza also worsens metabolic control (stress response raises glucose and triglycerides). Annual flu vaccination strongly recommended for all NAFLD/ALD patients.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Use inactivated (killed) influenza vaccine — NOT live attenuated (FluMist) in immunocompromised cirrhotic patients

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: PCV20 single dose or PCV15 then PPSV23 at 1 year; booster at 5 years for cirrhosis
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Cirrhosis causes profound immune dysfunction — bacterial infections (including pneumococcal pneumonia) are a leading cause of hospitalisation and death in cirrhosis. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is partly caused by gram-positive organisms. Pneumococcal vaccination significantly reduces serious pneumococcal disease risk in cirrhosis.
vaccinations_recommended.priority: HIGH PRIORITY for all cirrhotic patients; strongly recommended for advanced NAFLD

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: As per national guidelines; annual boosters in immunocompromised/cirrhosis
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients with NAFLD (especially with obesity, T2DM, and cirrhosis) have significantly higher COVID-19 morbidity and mortality. COVID-19 causes direct hepatic injury (SARS-CoV-2 infects ACE2-expressing hepatocytes) and triggers cytokine storm worsening liver inflammation. Vaccination dramatically reduces severe COVID-19 risk.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Cirrhotic patients generate lower antibody responses — may need additional doses; monitor antibody response

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Varicella Zoster Vaccine (Shingrix — Zoster Vaccine Recombinant)
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose course (0 and 2-6 months) for adults ≥50 years
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Immunocompromised patients (including those with cirrhosis) have higher risk of herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation and more severe disease. Shingrix is a non-live recombinant vaccine — SAFE even in immunocompromised patients (unlike live zoster vaccine Zostavax — contraindicated in severe immunocompromise).
vaccinations_recommended.note: Use Shingrix (recombinant, adjuvanted) NOT Zostavax (live-attenuated) in cirrhosis or immunocompromised NAFLD patients

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 3 doses at 0, 1, 6 months OR 4 doses at 0, 7 days, 21 days, 12 months (accelerated schedule for rapid protection)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Provides simultaneous protection against both hepatitis A and B — two infections that are potentially fatal in pre-existing liver disease. A single combined vaccine series improves adherence compared to two separate vaccine courses.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Preferred when both HAV and HBV non-immunity identified — efficient combined approach

when_to_see_doctor: Abnormal liver function tests (elevated ALT/AST) found on routine blood tests — especially in patients with obesity, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, or heavy alcohol use
Incidental finding of 'fatty liver' or increased liver echogenicity on abdominal ultrasound
Persistent unexplained fatigue and right upper quadrant discomfort
Diagnosed with metabolic syndrome (≥3 of: central obesity, high triglycerides, low HDL, high blood pressure, high fasting glucose) — liver assessment warranted
Heavy alcohol use — any alcohol-related symptoms warrant hepatology evaluation
Jaundice (yellowing of skin or eyes) — urgent evaluation required
Abdominal swelling or weight gain in abdominal area — possible ascites
ALT or AST rising trend on repeat blood tests — needs investigation
FIB-4 score >1.3 calculated from routine blood tests — hepatology or FibroScan referral needed
New onset type 2 diabetes — liver screen recommended (70% of T2DM have NAFLD)
Planning to start methotrexate, amiodarone, or tamoxifen — baseline liver assessment and monitoring plan needed
Obese child or adolescent — screening for paediatric NAFLD
Known NAFLD patient with worsening symptoms, new jaundice, swelling, confusion, or blood in vomit or stools — URGENT evaluation
Annual review for patients on established pharmacotherapy (pioglitazone — LFTs, oedema; resmetirom — LFTs; GLP-1 agonists — tolerance)
emergency_signs: Vomiting blood (haematemesis) — bright red or coffee-ground — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY — variceal haemorrhage in portal hypertension (up to 40% mortality per episode without treatment)
Black, tarry, foul-smelling stools (melaena) — upper GI bleeding from varices — EMERGENCY
Sudden confusion, drowsiness, or unconsciousness in a patient with liver disease — HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES
Severe abdominal pain with fever and ascites — SPONTANEOUS BACTERIAL PERITONITIS (SBP) — life-threatening infection
Rapidly increasing abdominal distension with breathlessness — tense ascites or acute liver decompensation
Jaundice appearing or rapidly worsening in a patient with known liver disease or alcoholic hepatitis — acute liver decompensation
Right upper quadrant pain with high fever and jaundice after heavy alcohol use — SEVERE ALCOHOLIC HEPATITIS — hospital admission required
Jaundice, confusion, and abdominal pain in a pregnant woman in the third trimester — ACUTE FATTY LIVER OF PREGNANCY — obstetric emergency — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES
Collapse or near-collapse with low blood pressure in a patient with liver disease — hepatorenal syndrome or septic shock
Significant unintentional weight loss (>5kg) in a patient with known NAFLD — possible hepatocellular carcinoma — urgent investigation

frequently_asked_questions.question: What exactly is fatty liver disease and is it serious?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Fatty liver disease means abnormal fat accumulation in the liver — more than 5% of liver cells contain fat. It has a wide spectrum: at one end, simple steatosis (just fat, no damage) which is reversible with lifestyle changes and generally not serious. At the other end, NASH/MASH (fat + inflammation + injury), which can progress over 10-20 years to cirrhosis and liver cancer. The good news: the majority of people with simple fatty liver do NOT progress to serious liver disease if they make lifestyle changes early. The bad news: it is often silent — no symptoms until advanced. This is why liver function tests and ultrasounds are important screening tools.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between NAFLD, MASLD, and NASH?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: NAFLD (Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease) is the older term — replaced by MASLD (Metabolic dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease) in 2023. MASLD means fatty liver linked to metabolic risk factors (obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, abnormal lipids). NASH (Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis) — now called MASH — is the severe inflammatory subtype of NAFLD/MASLD. So: MASLD = the broad disease category (fatty liver + metabolic risk); MASH = the severe form with inflammation and cell injury that can progress to cirrhosis and cancer. About 25% of MASLD patients have MASH.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can fatty liver be reversed?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — simple fatty liver (steatosis) is fully reversible with lifestyle changes. Even NASH/MASH — the more severe inflammatory form — can be reversed if caught before advanced fibrosis. Clinical trials show: 5% weight loss reduces liver fat significantly; 7% weight loss resolves NASH histologically in ~50% of patients; 10% weight loss improves fibrosis in most patients. The key is sustained lifestyle change — the liver has remarkable regenerative capacity. Even in patients with early cirrhosis (F4), stopping alcohol or achieving significant weight loss can halt progression and occasionally improve fibrosis.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I was told I have fatty liver on ultrasound. What should I do?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: First: don't panic — most people with fatty liver on ultrasound have simple steatosis (reversible). Your doctor should: (1) Check liver function blood tests (ALT, AST, GGT); (2) Calculate FIB-4 score from your blood tests to assess fibrosis risk; (3) Screen for underlying causes — diabetes (HbA1c, fasting glucose), cholesterol, triglycerides, thyroid function, viral hepatitis; (4) If FIB-4 >1.3 — refer for FibroScan (liver stiffness test). You should: Start a Mediterranean diet; eliminate sugary beverages (especially juices and fizzy drinks); start regular exercise; lose 5-10% body weight; stop or drastically reduce alcohol; drink 2-3 cups of coffee daily (hepatoprotective). Follow up with your doctor in 3-6 months.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is fatty liver linked to diabetes?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Very strongly — the bidirectional relationship between NAFLD and type 2 diabetes is one of the most important in hepatology. Approximately 70% of type 2 diabetes patients have NAFLD; 30-40% have NASH. Conversely, NAFLD significantly increases the risk of developing T2DM through hepatic insulin resistance. Each worsens the other: diabetes accelerates NASH fibrosis progression; NAFLD worsens glycaemic control through hepatic insulin resistance. If you have T2DM and have not had your liver assessed, ask your doctor for liver function tests, FIB-4 score calculation, and a liver ultrasound. Preferred antidiabetic drugs in NAFLD with T2DM: GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) and SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) — they treat both diabetes AND NAFLD.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is there any medication approved for fatty liver disease?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — resmetirom (Rezdiffra) was FDA-approved in March 2024 — the first ever drug specifically approved for MASH (non-alcoholic steatohepatitis). It is a thyroid hormone receptor-beta agonist taken once daily. It is approved for non-cirrhotic MASH with moderate-to-severe fibrosis (F2-F3), confirmed by liver biopsy. However, lifestyle modification (diet + exercise + weight loss of 7-10%) remains the most powerful treatment for fatty liver — more effective than any single drug. Other evidence-based treatments include: pioglitazone (for diabetics with NASH); Vitamin E (for non-diabetics with biopsy-proven NASH); GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide — significant NASH benefit in trials); SGLT2 inhibitors (reduce liver fat in T2DM-NAFLD). A number of other drugs are in late Phase 3 trials (lanifibranor, obeticholic acid).

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why is coffee recommended for fatty liver?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Coffee is one of the most remarkable hepatoprotective substances ever studied. Multiple large epidemiological studies and meta-analyses consistently show: people who drink 2-3 cups of coffee daily have 40-50% lower risk of liver fibrosis progression; 40% lower risk of liver cancer (HCC); lower liver enzyme levels (ALT, AST, GGT); and lower liver stiffness on FibroScan. Both caffeinated AND decaffeinated coffee provide benefit (suggesting non-caffeine components — chlorogenic acids, polyphenols, and diterpenes — are important). Mechanisms include reducing hepatic inflammation, inhibiting liver stellate cell activation (antifibrotic), antioxidant effects, and reducing de novo lipogenesis. In a patient with fatty liver, 2-3 cups of coffee daily (without added sugar) is one of the simplest and most effective hepatoprotective interventions available.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is FibroScan and when do I need it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: FibroScan (transient elastography) is a non-invasive, painless, 10-minute test performed in clinic — a probe is placed on the skin over the liver and sends low-energy waves to measure liver stiffness (in kilopascals — kPa). Stiffer liver = more fibrosis. It also measures liver fat (via CAP — Controlled Attenuation Parameter). FibroScan is the most important non-invasive test for assessing how much scarring (fibrosis) is present in the liver. Normal liver: <7 kPa; significant fibrosis: 7-13 kPa; cirrhosis: >13-15 kPa. You need FibroScan when: FIB-4 score (from your blood tests) is 1.3-2.67 (indeterminate risk); or your doctor wants to stage your fatty liver disease before treatment decisions. It must be done fasting (2 hours) and not immediately after exercise. Results are available immediately.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can children get fatty liver disease?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — paediatric NAFLD has become a major health concern globally. It affects 3-10% of all children and 35-40% of obese children, making it the most common chronic liver disease in children in many countries. It is closely linked to childhood obesity, sugar-sweetened beverage consumption, and sedentary lifestyle. Children often have no symptoms — it is typically found incidentally via elevated ALT or liver ultrasound. The management focuses on family-based lifestyle intervention (dietary changes for the whole family; reducing screen time; increasing physical activity). Weight loss of 7-10% of body weight significantly improves liver function in children. Medications are not routinely used in children — lifestyle intervention is primary treatment.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How does alcohol cause liver damage?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Alcohol (ethanol) damages the liver through multiple mechanisms simultaneously: (1) Acetaldehyde toxicity — alcohol is metabolised to acetaldehyde (highly reactive) which forms protein and DNA adducts causing hepatocyte damage; (2) Oxidative stress — CYP2E1 enzyme produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) during alcohol metabolism; (3) Mitochondrial dysfunction — impairs fatty acid oxidation, causing fat accumulation; (4) Gut dysbiosis — alcohol disrupts the intestinal barrier, allowing bacterial endotoxins (LPS) to reach the liver via portal blood, activating Kupffer cells and driving inflammation; (5) Nutritional deficiencies — particularly thiamine (B1), folate, and zinc. The combination of these effects progresses from: alcoholic fatty liver (reversible) → alcoholic hepatitis (potentially fatal) → alcoholic cirrhosis (irreversible).

frequently_asked_questions.question: What diet is best for fatty liver disease?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The Mediterranean diet has the strongest evidence for NAFLD — it reduces liver fat, improves liver enzymes, and is associated with better metabolic outcomes. The core principles: (1) Eliminate sugar-sweetened beverages and added sugars completely — fructose is THE primary driver of hepatic fat; (2) Drink 2-3 cups of coffee daily (hepatoprotective); (3) Eat plenty of vegetables, legumes, and whole grains; (4) Use olive oil as the primary fat; (5) Eat fish 2-3 times/week; (6) Nuts (especially walnuts) daily; (7) Moderate amounts of lean protein; (8) Avoid refined carbohydrates, processed meats, and saturated fats; (9) Complete alcohol abstinence (or minimal). The most important dietary intervention is CALORIE REDUCTION for weight loss — any dietary pattern that achieves 7-10% weight loss significantly improves NAFLD.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What are the warning signs that fatty liver is getting worse?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Simple fatty liver is usually asymptomatic. As it progresses, warning signs include: Persistent fatigue disproportionate to lifestyle; Right upper quadrant (upper right abdomen) ache or heaviness; Jaundice (yellowing of eyes or skin) — URGENT sign; Swollen abdomen (ascites — fluid accumulation) or leg swelling; Easy bruising or prolonged bleeding; Confusion or disorientation (hepatic encephalopathy); Blood in vomit (haematemesis) or black stools (melaena) — EMERGENCY. On blood tests: rising AST/ALT; falling platelets (thrombocytopenia — portal hypertension); rising bilirubin; prolonged INR; rising creatinine. On FibroScan: increasing liver stiffness. See your doctor promptly for any of these features.
